# EMC Website Design & Engineering Enhancement Plan

## 1. Executive Summary

The EMC rebuild has real bones: a disciplined design-token system with documented WCAG contrast math, a genuinely strong home hero with editorial photography, an accessible form primitive, and a content architecture that refuses to fabricate stats or testimonials — which matters more for this audience (MOH/NUPCO procurement, hospital administrators, biomedical engineers) than for a typical B2B site. On its best page, the site already reads at the Medtronic/Stryker tier it's aiming for.

But right now the site does not reliably show that page to a first-time visitor. A single confirmed, reproducible bug (`src/components/motion/reveal.tsx`) can leave the home hero headline, both primary CTA buttons, and the entire Contact form at near-zero opacity for several seconds — or indefinitely — until the visitor scrolls. That bug sits on exactly the three surfaces the site exists to convert on. Layered beneath it, every page that should carry the "real technology partner" story — About, all five Solution pages, all Partner pages, Product detail — substitutes an abstract gradient placeholder for photography, so even once the scroll bug is fixed, a buyer clicking past the homepage currently lands on pages that look unfinished rather than credible.

**Headline recommendation:** fix the Reveal bug and its accessibility corollaries this week — it is fully within engineering's control, well understood, and unanimous across all seven review lenses as the top priority. In parallel, begin sourcing real photography for the three pages the business's own content already substantiates (About, Anesthesia & Airway Management, UE Medical), since that is the next-most-damaging gap to the credibility story and the one that can't be fixed in code. Everything else in this plan is sequenced around those two facts.

---

## 2. What Is Already Working

This is not a site starting from zero — the following should be protected and built on, not redone:

- **The home hero clears the stated visual bar.** Real editorial OR photography, generous whitespace, purple/teal used only as a restrained accent (eyebrow label, one CTA) — this is the strongest single screen on the site and a legitimate reference for what interior pages should look like (`src/components/sections/home/hero.tsx`).
- **Anti-fabrication discipline is structural, not just a convention.** `TestimonialsSection` and `StatsBand` both `return null` rather than render placeholder content when verified data is absent; `partner-tile.tsx` falls back to a clean wordmark instead of a fake logo. For a fact-checking technical audience, this restraint is itself a trust signal.
- **Documented, verified WCAG contrast work.** `src/app/globals.css` contains inline comments with real contrast-ratio math (teal-700 = 4.91:1 for body text vs. teal-600 = 3.66:1 reserved for icons/large text) — independently recomputed during this review and confirmed accurate. This is more rigor than most B2B rebuilds do.
- **`src/components/ui/form-field.tsx` is a well-built accessible form primitive** — it clones `aria-invalid`/`aria-describedby` onto the input and pairs errors with `role="alert"`, covering both first-appearance and re-focus cases.
- **`customer-marquee.tsx` is genuinely well engineered** — pauses on hover/focus/drag, falls back to a static wrapped grid under `prefers-reduced-motion`, and carries 22 real, named hospital/institution logos (NUPCO, Sulaiman Al Habib, King Saud Medical City, PSMMC, etc.) — real social proof, not filler.
- **Every Solution/Product/Partner detail page consistently ends in a `CtaBand`** (Quotation Request + Contact), so a visitor who reaches the bottom of any detail page always has a clear next step — the "never end in nothing" rule is followed for the site's core content types, even where the listing pages one level up don't yet follow it.
- **Lead-gen forms collect fields that match how real institutional buyers work** — organization, job title, department, `procurementType: 'tender'|'direct'` — reflecting real NUPCO/MOH procurement literacy, not generic consumer form fields.
- **Copy has genuinely executed the "partner, not distributor" repositioning.** The word "distributor" does not appear anywhere in shipped content; hero and About copy consistently lead with training, technical support, regulatory knowledge (SFDA), and after-sales service. The AMECO partner correction and Partners cross-sell content give real specifics (1984 founding, 30,000 sqm facility, ISO 13485:2016) rather than vague "trusted partner" filler.
- **Breadcrumbs and RTL groundwork are done correctly** — `page-breadcrumb.tsx` mirrors chevrons for RTL, emits `BreadcrumbList` JSON-LD, and `html lang`/`dir` are correctly set per locale in the root layout.

---

## 3. P0 — Fix Now

These are unanimous or near-unanimous across the seven-lens review, shippable in code this week, and sit directly on the site's conversion surfaces.

### 3.1 Fix the Reveal/RevealGroup scroll-gating bug and decouple focus/pointer-events from opacity everywhere
**Files:** `src/components/motion/reveal.tsx`, plus every consumer — `src/components/sections/home/hero.tsx`, `src/app/[locale]/contact/page.tsx`, `src/app/[locale]/solutions/[slug]/page.tsx`, `src/app/[locale]/about/page.tsx`, ~30 files total. Also `src/components/layout/back-to-top.tsx`.

**What's happening:** `Reveal`/`RevealGroup` use Framer Motion's `whileInView` with `viewport={{ once: true, margin: "-80px" }}` and no synchronous fallback. Per `node_modules/framer-motion`'s own implementation, this is a thin wrapper over a shared native `IntersectionObserver` with no `getBoundingClientRect()` check — the hidden→visible flip depends entirely on the browser delivering an async callback, which can stall indefinitely on an idle page and resolves instantly on any scroll (exactly the reproduced symptom). It's applied to content that is guaranteed to already be in the viewport on load: the hero headline/subhead/CTA row in `hero.tsx`, and the entire Contact form in `contact/page.tsx`.

**Why it's P0, unanimously:** it suppresses the home hero headline and both primary CTA buttons, and the entire Contact form, on first paint — the three surfaces the site exists to convert on. Accessibility compounds this: wrapped elements remain fully keyboard-focusable while invisible, so a sighted keyboard user can tab into (and even type into) a Contact form field they cannot see. The back-to-top button has the identical focusable-but-invisible pattern independently.

**Fix:**
- For guaranteed above-the-fold content (hero, Contact form), replace `whileInView` with mount-time `animate="visible"` — no observer dependency, same variants/timing.
- For genuine below-the-fold content, harden with an imperative `useInView` + synchronous `getBoundingClientRect()` fallback on mount (the pattern `stat-counter.tsx` already uses correctly elsewhere in this codebase).
- As defense-in-depth, everywhere `Reveal` is used: tie `pointer-events`/focusability to the same visible state so nothing is ever focusable while at `opacity:0`. Apply the same fix to `back-to-top.tsx` (add `tabIndex={visible ? 0 : -1}` / `aria-hidden={!visible}`).

### 3.2 Restore a Request-a-Demo CTA on mobile
**Files:** `src/components/layout/header.tsx` (line ~55-57), `src/components/layout/mobile-nav.tsx` (lines ~43-98)

`header.tsx` wraps `<DemoRequestModal />` in `hidden sm:block` — it does not render at all below ~640px. `mobile-nav.tsx`'s hamburger Sheet contains only navigation links; no Demo/Quotation/Contact CTA anywhere inside it. A phone visitor — a very plausible access pattern for this audience via a shared link or WhatsApp forward — currently has zero header-level path to the site's flagship lead-gen action. Add a compact icon-only trigger at all widths, or a persistent CTA pinned inside the mobile Sheet.

### 3.3 Add a genuine 44px+ CTA size and apply it to every Demo/Quotation/Contact trigger
**File:** `src/components/ui/button.tsx`

No size in the current scale reaches the 44px touch-target baseline (`default` = 32px, `lg` = 36px), and the header's repeated CTA defaults to the smallest `sm` size (28px) — the single most-repeated button on the site. Add a genuinely larger size (h-11/44px+, more generous horizontal padding) reserved for hero and CTA-band primary actions, and apply it to every Demo/Quotation/Contact trigger sitewide, including the header default. This is both a usability failure (touch-target minimum) and a visual-weight failure (undersized CTAs read as "an app control, not a considered invitation" against the Medtronic/Stryker bar) — one fix addresses both.

### 3.4 Remove the non-functional "coming soon" search input
**File:** `src/components/layout/search-trigger.tsx`

The header search icon opens a Popover containing a permanently `disabled` input labeled "coming soon," live on every page. For a technical audience evaluating operational maturity, a visibly broken control undercuts the credibility goal more than a missing feature would. Remove it until the Fuse.js index actually has content to search.

### 3.5 Close the form-accessibility gap (bundled sweep)
**Files:** `src/components/ui/form-field.tsx`, `src/components/layout/demo-request-modal.tsx`, `quotation-request-modal.tsx`, `src/components/sections/contact/contact-form.tsx`, `src/components/sections/careers/application-form.tsx`, `src/components/layout/language-switcher.tsx`, `src/components/ui/dialog.tsx` (line 75)

Four small, same-family fixes to components the team already built well:
- Add `role="status"` (or `aria-live="polite"`) to all four forms' success-confirmation blocks — currently only the error path uses `role="alert"`; success gets no screen-reader announcement at all (fails SC 4.1.3).
- Propagate the `required` prop through to `aria-required`/native `required` on the underlying input — currently required fields are marked only by a colored asterisk glyph.
- Fix the language switcher's `aria-label` ("Language"/"اللغة") to match its visible text ("العربية"/"English") — currently fails SC 2.5.3 Label in Name on the one control whose job is helping Arabic-preferring users find it.
- Wrap the hardcoded English `"Close"` string in `dialog.tsx` in `lang="en"` (or localize it), since it renders unchanged inside Arabic-locale dialogs.

This matters disproportionately here because a WCAG 2.1 AA conformance statement is plausibly a hard requirement in MOH/NUPCO tender documentation, and the error-path pattern this needs to mirror is already correctly built.

## 4. P1 — Next

### 4.1 Source real photography for About, Anesthesia & Airway Management, and the UE Medical partner page
**Component:** `src/components/sections/gradient-mesh.tsx` (its own code comment: *"Stand-in for editorial photography (none supplied yet)"*), used in `about/page.tsx`, `solutions/[slug]/page.tsx`, `partners/[slug]/page.tsx`, `products/[slug]/page.tsx`

This is rated critical-to-medium by four lenses and is arguably as damaging to the "technology partner, not distributor" story as the Reveal bug — it just can't be fixed by editing a component. Total real photography in the codebase today is essentially 2 generic photos (Home) plus a handful of product shots for 3 SKUs; every other detail-page hero is a purple/teal gradient block. Scope this narrowly to the three pages the business itself already claims are fully substantiated (per `PROJECT_SPEC.md` Section 9.3) — About, Anesthesia & Airway Management, UE Medical — rather than all ~12 GradientMesh instances at once. Reserve GradientMesh for categories still honestly "expanding" (Critical Care, Respiratory Care), where the placeholder should read as "content pending," not as the site's default interior visual language.

### 4.2 Add a CtaBand to the bottom of every listing/index page; upgrade the Services card CTA
**Files:** `src/app/[locale]/solutions/page.tsx`, `products/page.tsx`, `partners/page.tsx`, `services/page.tsx`

Every `[slug]` detail page ends in the bold `CtaBand`; the index pages one level up — where a comparison-shopping visitor is most likely to be browsing before committing to one item — currently end in silence after the card grid. Separately, `services/page.tsx` (lines 72-79) renders each card's CTA as a plain, low-contrast underlined text link rendered only conditionally, in stark contrast to every other page type's gradient CTA band — notable because Services carries the clearest "technology partner not distributor" evidence on the site (Clinical Training, Installation, Commissioning, Maintenance & PM) and currently has the weakest CTA treatment of any page type.

### 4.3 Rebalance the Demo Request and Quotation Request modals via progressive disclosure
**Files:** `src/components/layout/demo-request-modal.tsx`, `quotation-request-modal.tsx`, `src/lib/validations/leads.ts`

Demo Request requires 9 fields (fullName, organization, jobTitle, department, city, email, mobile, preferredContactMethod, productOrSolutionOfInterest); Quotation Request requires 7 (organization, contactPerson, department, product, quantity, city, procurementType). Both are heavier than the site's own general Contact form (5 fields, 1 required beyond basics) — friction on the site's fastest "quick action" CTAs, at the exact first-touch moment friction most costs conversions.

These fields aren't arbitrary, though — job title, department, and `procurementType` are exactly the qualification data sales likely uses to route a NUPCO/MOH tender lead differently from a hospital walk-in inquiry, so deleting them trades conversion-rate optics for weaker leads downstream. **Resolution: progressive disclosure, not deletion.** Keep name/organization/email/mobile/interest as the only required first-screen fields; demote job title, department, city, and preferred-contact-method to optional or a second step. This preserves the qualification signal for leads willing to give it, without gating the "fastest path to a human" behind nine mandatory fields for everyone else.

### 4.4 Fix About page's brand-purple background violations
**File:** `src/app/[locale]/about/page.tsx`

`globals.css` documents its own rule: *"Surfaces are white/soft-gray dominant; purple and teal are accents only."* About uses solid `bg-emc-purple-900` as a full-bleed background three times — the hero (line 58), the Vision card (line 80), and the Corporate Philosophy band (line 162). This is drift from a rule the team already wrote down and enforces elsewhere, on the page most responsible for institutional credibility. Restyle the Vision card and Corporate Philosophy band using the neutral/teal-accent treatment already used on the Mission card; keep one deliberate purple field per page (the hero, once real photography lands).

### 4.5 Strengthen partner-relationship presentation
**Files:** `src/app/[locale]/solutions/[slug]/page.tsx` (lines 139-153), Partners index, home partners band

Three lenses independently flag the same gap from three surfaces: the Solution-detail page's related-Partners cross-sell cards are bare `border bg-card` boxes with no logo (a visibly different "species" of card from the icon-chip Solution/Product cards immediately surrounding them, despite the logo-with-wordmark-fallback pattern already existing via `PartnerTile`); the Partners index and homepage partners band render logo/name only, while the real substantiation (1984 founding, 30,000 sqm facility, ISO 13485:2016, CE) sits one click deeper. Give the cross-sell cards their partner logo, and surface one credibility fragment (founding year + one certification) directly under each logo on the homepage band and index, not only on detail pages — this is the core "partner not distributor" differentiator and is currently presented no differently than a bare distributor supplier-logo grid.

### 4.6 Add a Request a Quotation CTA to the Product detail hero
**File:** `src/app/[locale]/products/[slug]/page.tsx` (lines 106-121, CtaBand at line 343)

The hero CTA row currently offers only Demo / Specialist / Brochure; Quotation Request doesn't appear until the bottom `CtaBand`, after a full scroll through specs, certificates, and downloads. Given `procurementType: 'tender'|'direct'` is already a first-class field in the content model, and this audience is plausibly tender-driven, add Quotation to the hero row alongside the existing three.

### 4.7 Verify P0/P1 fixes on real mobile viewports and the `/ar` RTL route
Four lenses independently flagged mobile and RTL rendering as unconfirmed this session (the review tool could not reliably render below desktop width). Treat this as a required release gate — not a someday item — for the Reveal fix, the touch-target fix, and the mobile-CTA fix specifically, before marking any of them done. `GradientMesh` and `Reveal` are the same shared, non-locale-conditional components on `/ar` routes, so the critical findings above very likely reproduce there but were not confirmed on-screen.

## 5. P2 — Later / Strategic Bets

- **Add the missing Partners link to the footer's Quick Links column** — `partnersMenu` is already imported and used elsewhere in the codebase; Solutions was explicitly hand-added to the footer list but Partners was not (`src/components/layout/footer.tsx`, lines 55-74). One-line fix, low business impact relative to P0/P1, so it's sequenced after them rather than displacing them.
- **Replace the generic icon-chip card template with representative photography per category** (Solutions grid, Products grid, About pillars) — named by three lenses as the design system's own documented anti-pattern ("large rounded-corner icons above every heading... screams template"). Explicitly gated behind 4.1 (photography sourcing) landing first — redesigning these cards before assets exist means redoing the work twice. Start with Anesthesia & Airway Management once its photography exists.
- **Promote 3-4 substantiated Why-EMC pillars (Training, Regulatory Knowledge/SFDA, Technical Support, After-Sales) into a compact homepage module**, replacing the current single-paragraph teaser (`src/components/sections/home/why-emc-teaser.tsx`). The real, spec-compliant content already exists in `content/pages/about.json` but is gated behind a second click most first-pass visitors won't take — high positioning value, but a content-layout project of its own, appropriately sequenced after active defects are fixed.
- **Reframe Products listing copy** ("Browse Our Products" → "Featured Products") and grow real catalog depth beyond 3 SKUs. A 3-item catalog framed as the full browse experience undersells the business, but growing it is a manufacturer-coordination/inventory task, not a design or engineering fix.
- **Add route-level `loading.tsx`/Suspense fallbacks** ahead of the spec's own planned Sanity CMS migration. No `loading.tsx` exists anywhere in `src/app/[locale]/**` today; currently masked because content reads from fast synchronous local JSON, but the planned CMS migration will introduce real network latency into the same zero-fallback route structure. Correctly pre-work for that migration, not an urgent fix now.
- **Source real testimonials and confirmed stats** (years-of-experience, product count, partner count) to populate the two homepage sections (`StatsBand`, `TestimonialsSection`) that currently render nothing, correctly gated by the anti-fabrication rule. This is a business/content-acquisition task — the code path to display the data the moment it's supplied is already built and compliant.

## 6. Open Items Not Verified This Session

- **True mobile/small-viewport rendering.** The browser tool used this session could not reliably force sub-desktop viewport widths. Reviewed responsively from Tailwind breakpoints in source (which generally look reasonable — e.g., `MobileNav`'s Sheet/Accordion uses standard Base UI primitives with an `aria-label`'d trigger), but touch-target sizing, focus-trap behavior, and the Demo/Quotation modals' `max-h-[85vh]` + internal scroll behavior with an on-screen keyboard open were not observed live. **Recommendation:** a real-device or Chrome DevTools responsive-mode pass (with touch emulation) against the mobile nav Sheet, both lead-gen modals, and the Contact form, specifically re-run after the P0 fixes land.
- **`/ar` Arabic RTL rendering of the P0/P1 items above.** `GradientMesh` and `Reveal` are shared, non-locale-conditional components, so the Reveal bug and photography gap very likely reproduce identically on `/ar` — but this was inferred from code, not confirmed on-screen. **Recommendation:** verify on the live `/ar` route once fixes ship, given this audience plausibly accesses the site Arabic-first.
- **`useReducedMotion()` hydration-timing behavior.** Framer Motion's `useReducedMotion` reads `window.matchMedia` synchronously during render rather than inside a `useEffect`, which is a theoretical SSR/client hydration-mismatch risk specifically for visitors with OS-level "reduce motion" enabled — exactly the accessibility-conscious users this code path exists to serve correctly. **Recommendation:** a quick manual check (DevTools "Emulate CSS prefers-reduced-motion: reduce" + hard reload on a Reveal-heavy page, watching for console hydration warnings) to confirm whether this is purely theoretical or produces a visible flash in practice.
- **Header CTA/search/language-switcher absence on very first paint.** One screenshot captured on a fresh load showed the header ending at "Contact" with no search icon, language switcher, or Demo button visible, while later screenshots (post-scroll/navigation) show all three consistently. This is distinct from the diagnosed Reveal bug (these components have no opacity-hiding logic) and is more consistent with a hydration-timing race on Base UI's portal-based components. **Recommendation:** investigate whether these three components SSR to an empty state before hydration completes, and if so, render a static non-interactive placeholder server-side so the header CTA is never absent on first paint.

## 7. Appendix: Full Per-Lens Findings

### 7.1 Frontend Engineering Quality
**Summary:** Codebase is disciplined overall (typed content getters, CVA button system, a properly spec-compliant lead-gen modal with loading/success/error states and full a11y wiring, a minimal scroll-condense header). The confirmed Reveal bug has a traceable architectural root cause: `whileInView` has no synchronous "already visible" check and is misapplied to guaranteed-above-fold content.

- **Critical** — Reveal's `whileInView` architecture (no `getBoundingClientRect` fallback) applied to guaranteed above-fold content in `hero.tsx` (eyebrow/headline/subhead/CTA row/hero image). *Fix: mount-time `animate` for above-fold; hardened `useInView` + `getBoundingClientRect` fallback below fold.*
- **High** — `RevealGroup`'s `stagger` prop is dead code at all ~15+ call sites because each nested `Reveal` child independently triggers its own `whileInView` instead of inheriting parent variant orchestration; the visible stagger effect actually comes from three different hand-typed `delay={i * magicNumber}` conventions duplicated across `solutions-grid.tsx`, `stats-band.tsx`, `careers/page.tsx`. *Fix: either make Reveal context-aware of RevealGroup, or delete the unused `stagger` prop and codify one `STAGGER_STEP` constant.*
- **Medium** — No route-level `loading.tsx`/Suspense boundary anywhere in `src/app/[locale]/**`; masked today by synchronous local-JSON reads, but the spec's planned Sanity CMS migration will introduce real latency into the same zero-fallback structure.
- **Low** — `useReducedMotion()` reads `window.matchMedia` synchronously at render, not effect-gated — theoretical SSR hydration-mismatch risk for reduced-motion users specifically.

**Strengths:** `demo-request-modal.tsx` (loading/success/error states, Zod+RHF validation, aria wiring, delayed reset-on-close); `button.tsx`'s clean CVA system and correct polymorphic `render` prop usage; `header.tsx`'s minimal scroll-condense (single passive listener, CSS-driven interpolation); `stat-counter.tsx`'s correct `useReducedMotion` branch + RAF cleanup; `nav.ts`'s single-source-of-truth `solutionIcons` export.

### 7.2 UX / Usability Heuristics
**Summary:** Sound IA and above-average form accessibility engineering, but the lead-gen funnel has real friction: dense modals heavier than the general Contact form, undersized touch targets sitewide, a vanishing mobile CTA, and a weak Services CTA next to bold CtaBands elsewhere.

- **Critical** — Primary Demo CTA hidden below `sm` breakpoint (`header.tsx` lines 55-57) with no replacement in `mobile-nav.tsx`'s Sheet.
- **Critical** — Reveal bug hits the Home hero CTA row and the entire Contact form specifically.
- **High** — No button size reaches 44px (`button.tsx`: default 32px, sm 28px, lg 36px); header's repeated CTA defaults to `sm` (28px).
- **High** — Demo (9 required fields) and Quotation (7 required fields) modals heavier than the general Contact form (5 fields, 1 required).
- **Medium** — Services page CTA is a plain conditional text link, unlike every other detail page's `CtaBand` (`services/page.tsx` lines 72-79).
- **Medium** — Footer omits a Partners link even though `partnersMenu` is imported and Solutions was hand-added to the same list (`footer.tsx` lines 55-74).
- **Medium** — Header search opens a permanently `disabled` input labeled "coming soon" (`search-trigger.tsx`).
- **Low** — Demo/Quotation modals' `max-h-[85vh]` + internal scroll risk double-scrolling on short viewports with keyboard open (unverified).

**Strengths:** `form-field.tsx`'s aria wiring; mega-menu reduces large sitemap without losing category access; Services→Contact `?type=` prefill (`contact/page.tsx` lines 14-22) is thoughtful funnel engineering; Contact form itself is appropriately lightweight; RTL-correct breadcrumbs with JSON-LD; consistent `CtaBand` on all detail-page types.

### 7.3 Visual Taste and Craft Polish
**Summary:** Real design-system discipline (documented WCAG color tokens, consistent `py-16 sm:py-24` section rhythm, refusal to fabricate testimonials/logos) that breaks down once you leave Home: a repeated icon-chip card template and the GradientMesh photography placeholder dominate every interior page.

- **Critical** — GradientMesh (`gradient-mesh.tsx`, self-documented as a photography stand-in) on About hero and every Solution/Product/Partner detail page.
- **High** — Identical icon-in-teal-square card template across `solution-card.tsx`, `product-card.tsx`, `about/pillar-card.tsx`, `services/page.tsx`, `desktop-nav.tsx` — five clinically distinct categories rendered interchangeable.
- **Medium** — Solution-detail Partners cross-sell cards are bare bordered boxes with no logo, inconsistent with surrounding icon-chip cards (`solutions/[slug]/page.tsx` lines 139-153).
- **Medium** — About page uses full-bleed `bg-emc-purple-900` three times (hero, Vision card, Corporate Philosophy band), against the codebase's own documented "accents only" rule.
- **Medium** — Reveal bug compounds with GradientMesh on Solution-detail heroes to produce a near-blank first impression (screenshot-confirmed on Anesthesia & Airway Management).
- **Low** — No CTA size beyond 36px in `button.tsx`.

**Strengths:** Documented, real WCAG contrast-ratio math in `globals.css`; consistent section vertical rhythm across Home/About/Solutions/Products/Partners; `testimonials-section.tsx`/`partner-tile.tsx` refuse to fabricate content; Home hero h1 (`text-6xl`) intentionally scaled up vs. interior-page h1s (`text-5xl`); uniform hover/focus-visible states across all card types.

### 7.4 Premium Editorial Visual-Brand Fit
**Summary:** The design system (tokens, spacing, restrained-accent rule, motion primitives) is disciplined and clears the Medtronic/Stryker bar on Home specifically — but the site has almost no real photography anywhere else (6 photographic assets total in the entire codebase, 2 of them on Home).

- **Critical** — Reveal bug leaves hero and body text near-invisible on load sitewide.
- **Critical** — Zero real photography beyond Home; GradientMesh substitutes on About, all 5 Solution details, Product detail, Partner detail.
- **High** — Product catalog too thin (3 SKUs) to read as a real catalog; ProductCard falls back to a generic icon square whenever `heroImage` is absent.
- **Medium** — Partners section still a logo-plus-paragraph card grid with no facility/device imagery — "the literal pattern named in the brief as the thing to move away from."
- **Medium** — Icon system on Solutions/Products listing generic and interchangeable, not distinctive enough to carry pages lacking photography.
- **Low** — Interior-page hero "white space" currently reads as unfinished placeholder, not intentional restraint, because it's an empty gradient box rather than content-adjacent breathing room.
- **Low** — Mobile rendering of these issues unverified this session.

**Strengths:** Home hero genuinely hits the stated bar; documented WCAG-driven color-contrast decisions in `globals.css`; token architecture correctly enforces "purple/teal as accent only" at the CSS variable level; `CustomerMarquee`'s restrained, accessible engineering; anti-fabrication discipline as a trust signal; Products/Solutions listing page layout skeletons have correct editorial breathing room even where content inside them is thin.

### 7.5 Accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA)
**Summary:** An above-average accessibility effort for a site this size — verified contrast math, a working skip link, a reduced-motion-aware marquee, and a well-built form-error pattern. The Reveal bug is the most consequential defect for this lens specifically because it leaves interactive elements focusable-but-invisible, a materially worse failure mode than cosmetic animation.

- **Critical** — Reveal bug leaves focusable, sometimes typeable, invisible content sitewide (30 files), including all Contact form fields.
- **High** — Form success states across all four lead-gen forms lack `role="status"`/`aria-live` (fails SC 4.1.3); error path correctly uses `role="alert"`, showing the team knows the pattern but didn't apply it symmetrically.
- **Medium** — `required` prop never propagated to `aria-required`/native `required` anywhere in the codebase — conveyed only via a colored asterisk glyph.
- **Medium** — Language switcher `aria-label` ("Language") doesn't match its visible text ("العربية"/"English") — fails SC 2.5.3.
- **Low** — Hardcoded, unlocalized "Close" string in `dialog.tsx` line 75 renders inside Arabic-locale dialogs with no `lang` annotation.
- **Low** — Back-to-top button remains keyboard-focusable while visually hidden — same focusable-but-invisible anti-pattern as Reveal, independently.
- **Low** — Mobile touch-target sizing and MobileNav Sheet/Accordion focus-trap behavior unverified live this session (source looks reasonable).

**Strengths:** `globals.css` WCAG comments independently recomputed and confirmed accurate; focus rings correctly use `--ring` (teal-700, 4.9:1); `form-field.tsx`'s dual first-appearance/re-focus error handling; `customer-marquee.tsx`'s strong SC 2.2.2 implementation; `gradient-mesh.tsx` correctly sets `aria-hidden` when purely decorative; genuinely descriptive product alt text (e.g., "UEScope video laryngoscope handle with an integrated monitor showing an endoscopic airway view"); correct per-locale `lang`/`dir`; `StatCounter` correctly jumps to final value under reduced motion rather than merely slowing.

### 7.6 Conversion / Lead-Generation Optimization
**Summary:** Detail-page lead-gen mechanics (Solution/Product/Partner) are well built — consistent CtaBand, correct CTA hierarchy in the product hero, procurement-literate form fields, zero fabricated trust content. Conversion is capped by three things: no CTA on index/listing pages, the Reveal bug sitting on the home hero and the Products listing's real photography, and the hidden mobile header CTA.

prioritized.panel_notes:
Seven lenses converged fast on one thing: the Reveal.tsx scroll bug is the top priority, unanimously, because it sits on the hero, the primary CTAs, and the Contact form simultaneously — the exact three surfaces the site exists to convert on. There was no dissent to work through there; the only discussion was scope. Frontend-engineering's fix (mount-time `animate` for guaranteed-above-fold content, a hardened `useInView` + `getBoundingClientRect` fallback for genuine below-fold content) and accessibility's requirement (decouple focusability/pointer-events from opacity) are the same patch, not competing ones, so we merged them into a single P0 item and folded in the two other "focusable-but-invisible" instances the panel found independently (back-to-top button, and by extension any future Reveal-wrapped control) so engineering fixes the anti-pattern once, not three times.

The one real tension in the room was over the Demo/Quotation modals. UX-heuristics and conversion both want the 9-required-field Demo form and 7-field Quotation form shortened, arguing they're heavier than the site's own Contact form and add friction at the exact moment friction kills conversion. But the fields in question (job title, department, procurement type, preferred contact method) are load-bearing for how EMC's sales team actually qualifies a NUPCO/MOH tender lead versus a hospital walk-in inquiry — deleting them trades conversion-rate optics for weaker leads downstream, which nobody on the panel was willing to sign off on outright. We resolved it as progressive disclosure, not deletion: keep name/org/email/mobile/interest as the only required first-screen fields, demote job title/department/city/preferred-contact-method to optional or a second step. That preserves the qualification data for leads who give it while not gating the "fastest path to human contact" behind nine mandatory fields.

A second sequencing question came up rather than a disagreement: GradientMesh-as-photography-placeholder is called "critical" by four lenses and is arguably as damaging to the credibility story as the Reveal bug, but it is not something engineering can fix by editing a component — it requires sourcing or commissioning real photography. We kept it out of P0 (which we reserved for things shippable in code this week) and put it at the top of P1, scoped narrowly to the three pages the business itself already claims are substantiated (About, Anesthesia & Airway Management, UE Medical partner page) rather than all ~12 GradientMesh instances at once, so it's an achievable next sprint rather than an open-ended asset backlog. The generic icon-chip card template, catalog depth, and Why-EMC promotion are explicitly gated behind that same photography pipeline landing first, which is why they're P2 — sequencing them earlier would mean redesigning cards around assets that don't exist yet.

We also grouped several single-lens "low severity" a11y findings (missing aria-live on form success states, required fields never getting aria-required, language-switcher label mismatch, hardcoded English "Close" in RTL dialogs) into one P0/P1 sweep rather than treating them as isolated nitpicks — individually minor, but this audience includes MOH/NUPCO tenders where a WCAG conformance statement can be a hard requirement, and the fixes are all small, same-family changes to components the team already built well (form-field.tsx). Finally, the panel agreed mobile/RTL verification is not optional polish — four lenses flagged it as unconfirmed, and this audience plausibly accesses the site mobile-first and Arabic-first, so we placed it as a required verification gate immediately after the P0/P1 code fixes ship, not as a someday item.

themes.theme: Reveal.tsx scroll-animation bug leaves above-the-fold hero, CTAs, and the Contact form invisible on load
themes.description: The confirmed live bug in src/components/motion/reveal.tsx (whileInView + IntersectionObserver that frequently doesn't fire until a scroll gesture) is the single most-cited defect across all seven lenses. It was independently diagnosed from four different angles: frontend-engineering traced the architectural root cause (whileInView has no synchronous 'already in viewport' check, and is misapplied to guaranteed-above-fold content like the hero and Contact form); accessibility found it produces a strictly worse failure mode than cosmetic animation glitches — elements stay keyboard-focusable and even typeable while invisible; conversion and ux-heuristics both flag that it sits directly on the home hero headline/subhead/both primary CTA buttons and on the entire Contact form; taste-polish and brand-visual-system both note it compounds with the GradientMesh placeholder to make Solution-detail pages (e.g. Anesthesia & Airway Management, screenshot 8) look like a near-blank broken page; industry-fit frames it as directly undermining credibility at the exact moment a procurement/administrator visitor is deciding whether to trust the vendor.
themes.merged_findings: Root cause (frontend-engineering): whileInView is a thin wrapper over a shared native IntersectionObserver with no getBoundingClientRect fallback, so the hidden→visible flip depends on the browser electing to deliver an async callback; any scroll forces the paint/layout flush that delivers it, matching the observed 'resolves instantly on scroll' symptom. It is applied to content (hero.tsx eyebrow/headline/subhead/CTA row/hero image, Contact page form+sidebar) that is guaranteed to already be in the initial viewport and should never have been scroll-gated. Impact stacks across lenses: accessibility notes focusable-but-invisible form fields (a sighted keyboard user can tab into and fill fields they cannot see) with no ARIA state announcing the transition; conversion notes it suppresses the site's two highest-value conversion surfaces (home hero CTAs, Contact form) and visibly washes out the one page with real editorial photography (Products listing, screenshot 5, product photos rendering at ~15-20% opacity); taste-polish/brand-visual-system note the compounding effect with GradientMesh on Solution-detail heroes producing an apparently blank page. Recommended fix converges across lenses: for guaranteed-above-fold content, replace whileInView with mount-time `animate` (no observer dependency); for genuine below-fold content, harden with an imperative useInView + synchronous getBoundingClientRect check (as stat-counter.tsx already does); as defense-in-depth, decouple focusability/pointer-events from the opacity state so nothing is ever focusable while invisible.

single_lens_standouts: RevealGroup's `stagger` prop is dead code at every one of its ~15+ call sites because each nested Reveal child independently triggers its own whileInView instead of inheriting the parent's variant orchestration — the visible stagger effect actually comes from three different hand-typed `delay={i * magicNumber}` conventions duplicated across call sites (frontend-engineering).

No route-level loading.tsx or Suspense fallback exists anywhere in the app; currently masked by synchronous local-JSON content, but the spec's own planned Sanity CMS migration will introduce real network latency into the same zero-fallback route structure (frontend-engineering).

The Demo Request (9 required fields) and Quotation Request (7 required fields) modals — the site's flagship 'quick action' CTAs, triggered from every header and CTA band — are meaningfully heavier than the site's own general Contact form (5 fields, only 1 required beyond the basics), asking for job title/department/city/preferred-contact-method before a prospect has spoken to a human (ux-heuristics).

The footer's 'Quick Links' column explicitly appends a hand-added link to the Solutions menu but never adds one for Partners, even though partnersMenu is imported and used elsewhere in the codebase — Partners is reachable only via the top nav mega-menu or a deep link (ux-heuristics).

The header's search icon opens a Popover containing a permanently `disabled` input labeled 'coming soon' — a visibly non-functional decoy shipped live on every page rather than being removed until the Fuse.js index actually has content to search (ux-heuristics).

Form submission success states across all four lead-gen forms (Demo, Quotation, Contact, Careers) render with no role="status"/aria-live, so screen-reader users get no confirmation their submission succeeded — while the adjacent error path correctly uses role="alert", showing the team knows the pattern but didn't apply it symmetrically to success (accessibility).

Required form fields are indicated only by a colored asterisk glyph in FormField's rendering — the `required` prop is never propagated to the underlying input as `aria-required` or a native `required` attribute anywhere in the codebase (accessibility).

The language switcher's aria-label ('Language'/'اللغة') doesn't match its own visible button text ('العربية'/'English'), failing SC 2.5.3 Label in Name on the one control whose entire job is helping Arabic-preferring users find the toggle (accessibility).

The back-to-top button remains in the keyboard tab order and is only visually hidden via opacity/pointer-events when not yet scrolled past threshold — no tabIndex={-1} or aria-hidden gating — the same focusable-but-invisible anti-pattern as the Reveal bug, appearing a second time independently (accessibility).

The entire product catalog is 3 SKUs; ProductCard falls back to a generic icon square whenever heroImage is absent, and the listing page's 'Browse Our Products' framing doesn't signal that this is a partial/featured set rather than the whole inventory (brand-visual-system).

The About page uses solid brand-purple as a full-bleed background three separate times (hero, Vision card, Corporate Philosophy band), directly contradicting the codebase's own documented rule in globals.css that 'purple and teal are accents only' — notable because this is the page most responsible for institutional credibility (taste-polish).

On the Product detail hero, the Request a Quotation CTA — arguably the intent type most relevant to the site's actual procurement/tender-driven audience, and a first-class field (procurementType: tender|direct) in the content model itself — doesn't appear until the very bottom CtaBand, after a full scroll through specs/certificates/downloads; only Demo/Specialist/Brochure appear in the hero (conversion).

The homepage's 'Why EMC' section is reduced to a single eyebrow + headline + one paragraph + 'Learn more' link, even though the full 8-pillar substantiated content (Training, Regulatory Knowledge/SFDA, Technical Support, After-Sales) already exists in content/pages/about.json — the core 'partner not distributor' differentiator is gated behind a second click most first-pass visitors won't take (industry-fit).

content/stats.json (all three counters) and content/testimonials/ (empty) mean two of the homepage's nine sections currently render nothing — correctly compliant with the anti-fabrication rule, but a real content gap: the homepage has trust logos but no accompanying numbers or attributed voices to reinforce them (conversion).
cross_lens_strengths: Anti-fabrication discipline is structural, not just conventional: testimonials-section.tsx and StatsBand both return null rather than render placeholder content when verified data is absent, and partner-tile.tsx falls back to a clean wordmark rather than fabricating a logo — independently praised by taste-polish, brand-visual-system, conversion, and industry-fit as a genuine credibility asset for a fact-checking technical audience.

Documented, independently-verified WCAG contrast-ratio work in src/app/globals.css (teal-700 = 4.91:1 vs teal-600 = 3.66:1, correctly split between body text and icon/large-text use) — praised by accessibility (who recomputed and confirmed the numbers), taste-polish, and brand-visual-system as real engineering rigor most B2B rebuilds skip.

The Home hero is a genuine exemplar of the stated Medtronic/Stryker/Philips visual bar when real assets exist: large editorial photography, generous whitespace, purple/teal used only as restrained accents — independently singled out as the strongest single screen on the site by taste-polish, brand-visual-system, and industry-fit.

src/components/ui/form-field.tsx is a well-built accessible form primitive (clones aria-invalid/aria-describedby onto the input, pairs with role="alert" error text) — praised independently by frontend-engineering (as evidence of general engineering capability), ux-heuristics (as above-average for a B2B site), and accessibility (as covering both first-appearance and re-focus error cases).

customer-marquee.tsx is a well-engineered, restrained 'trusted by' component — pauses on hover/focus/drag, falls back to a static wrapped grid under prefers-reduced-motion — independently praised by brand-visual-system, accessibility (as a strong SC 2.2.2 implementation), and conversion (as genuinely relevant social proof, not filler, given the 22 real named hospital/institution logos it carries).

Every Solution/Product/Partner detail page consistently ends in the same CtaBand component (Quotation Request + Contact), giving a visitor who reaches the bottom of any detail page a clear next step — independently praised by ux-heuristics and conversion as evidence the 'never end in nothing' rule is followed for core content types, which sharpens the contrast with the listing/index pages that don't follow the same pattern.

reports.summary: The codebase is disciplined and largely well-structured for a Next.js 15 / React 19 / Tailwind v4 stack: typed content getters, a real CVA-based button/variant system, a properly spec-compliant lead-gen modal (loading/success/error states, Zod + RHF validation, a11y wiring), and a lightweight scroll-condense header. The one confirmed live bug (reveal.tsx opacity-stuck-until-scroll) has a traceable, code-level root cause in how Framer Motion's whileInView is architected and, more importantly, in where it is applied: it is used unconditionally on content — the hero, likely the Contact form — that is guaranteed to already be in the initial viewport and therefore should never have been gated behind scroll-triggered IntersectionObserver logic in the first place. A second, independent structural defect was found by reading reveal.tsx against its own call sites: RevealGroup's `stagger` prop is dead code at every one of its ~15+ usages because its Reveal children each run their own independent whileInView trigger instead of inheriting the parent's variant orchestration, so every call site has to hand-roll a duplicated `delay={i * constant}` instead. Overall the team is clearly capable (see the demo modal, the button primitive, StatCounter) — the gaps are concentrated in the motion layer, not general engineering discipline.
strengths: src/components/layout/demo-request-modal.tsx is a genuinely strong implementation of the spec's lead-gen requirement (Section 11): Button's built-in `loading` prop drives a spinner during submit, submission renders an inline success state with no page navigation, a separate inline error state, full Zod + react-hook-form validation with aria-invalid/aria-describedby wired to each field, a responsive `grid sm:grid-cols-2` layout, and a 200ms-delayed form reset on close so the visible form doesn't visibly flash back to empty mid-closing-transition.

src/components/ui/button.tsx: a clean CVA variant/size system, consistent focus-visible ring treatment, disabled-during-loading handling, and correct use of Base UI's polymorphic `render` prop to compose Link-as-button without a nested <a><button> anti-pattern (src/components/sections/home/hero.tsx:40 `render={<Link href="/solutions" />}`).

src/components/layout/header.tsx: the scroll-condense effect is minimal and correct — a single passive scroll listener toggling one boolean, with the actual visual interpolation (padding/border/logo height) handled by Tailwind transition classes rather than JS-driven style writes; good separation of concerns.

src/components/ui/stat-counter.tsx is a well-built, self-contained scroll-triggered counter: correctly branches on useReducedMotion, uses requestAnimationFrame with a proper easing curve, and cleans up its RAF on unmount — it just wasn't wired into the one place with real verified numbers (Featured Technology facts) until the docs/superpowers plan closed that gap.

src/lib/nav.ts's `solutionIcons` export, reused by both the mega-menu and ProductCard (per docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-18-ui-polish-animation-plan.md Task 3/4), is a genuine single-source-of-truth pattern rather than the icon mapping being copy-pasted per component.

findings.title: reveal.tsx whileInView bug: traced root cause is architectural, not incidental — above-the-fold content is scroll-gated when it should animate on mount
findings.evidence: Read node_modules/framer-motion/dist/es/motion/features/viewport/index.mjs (InViewFeature) and observers.mjs: whileInView is implemented as a thin wrapper over a plain, shared native IntersectionObserver — `mount()` calls `startObserver()` which calls `observeIntersection(...)`, and that's it. There is no synchronous 'is this element already on screen right now' check (e.g. no getBoundingClientRect fallback) — the hidden→visible transition depends entirely on the browser electing to deliver the observer's first callback, which per the IntersectionObserver spec/implementation is delivered asynchronously at the next paint/idle opportunity, not synchronously on `.observe()`. On an otherwise-idle page (a visitor who lands and reads without scrolling — exactly the confirmed repro), there may be no compositor/paint work scheduled to flush that pending callback, so it can stall indefinitely; any scroll event forces exactly the paint/layout flush that delivers it, which matches the confirmed 'resolves instantly on any scroll gesture' behavior precisely. Compounding this, reveal.tsx applies this scroll-gated mechanism to content that is guaranteed to be in the initial viewport: hero.tsx lines 25, 33, 38 wrap the eyebrow/headline, subhead, and CTA row each in `<Reveal>`, and line 47 wraps the `priority`-loaded LCP hero image in `<Reveal delay={0.1}>` too — none of this content is ever actually 'below the fold scrolled into view,' so whileInView was never the semantically correct tool for it; `initial`+`animate` (which runs unconditionally on mount, no observer involved) would have been.
findings.recommendation: Split Reveal's usage by fold position: for guaranteed-above-the-fold content (hero.tsx's three Reveals and image Reveal, and likely the Contact page's first form section), replace `whileInView`/`viewport` with `animate="visible"` (unconditional mount-time animation, same variants/timing, zero observer dependency) — this alone fixes the highest-visibility instance of the bug. For genuine below-the-fold Reveal usage, harden it the way stat-counter.tsx already does elsewhere in this codebase: call `useInView` imperatively and do a synchronous `getBoundingClientRect()` check on mount so elements already in view resolve immediately instead of waiting on the observer's async delivery. As cheap defense-in-depth regardless of the above, consider changing the `hidden` variant from `opacity: 0` to something less catastrophic (e.g. `opacity: 0.85`) so that even a stalled observer never renders a headline or form label as effectively invisible to a procurement reader.

findings.title: RevealGroup's `stagger` prop is dead code at every call site — the real stagger timing is duplicated by hand instead
findings.area: src/components/motion/reveal.tsx:43-67 (RevealGroup); all ~15+ call sites e.g. src/components/sections/home/solutions-grid.tsx:20-30, src/components/sections/home/stats-band.tsx:19-29, src/app/[locale]/careers/page.tsx:58-64
findings.evidence: RevealGroup sets `initial="hidden" whileInView="visible" transition={{staggerChildren: stagger}}` on a parent motion.div (reveal.tsx:57-62) — Framer Motion's staggerChildren orchestration only works when children subscribe to the parent's propagated variant state (i.e. children have a `variants` prop but no own trigger). But every RevealGroup call site nests `Reveal` children, and `Reveal` independently sets its own `initial="hidden" whileInView="visible" viewport={{once:true, margin:"-80px"}}` (reveal.tsx:32-34) — each child therefore triggers off its own independent intersection observation, not the parent's stagger orchestration, making RevealGroup's `stagger` parameter (default 0.08) inert everywhere it's used. The staggered appearance actually visible on screen comes entirely from manually-computed `delay={i * 0.06}` / `delay={i * 0.08}` / `delay={i * 0.05}` props passed to each Reveal individually (solutions-grid.tsx:24, stats-band.tsx:21, careers/page.tsx:60 — three different magic-number increments across three call sites, none reading from RevealGroup's stagger prop).
findings.recommendation: Pick one of two fixes rather than leaving the API self-contradictory: (a) make Reveal detect when it's nested inside a RevealGroup (e.g. via context) and drop its own initial/whileInView/viewport in that case, so it purely inherits the parent's propagated variants and RevealGroup's `stagger` prop starts actually doing something — then delete the duplicated `delay={i * constant}` from every call site; or (b) if per-child independent viewport triggering is actually desired (arguably more correct for a long grid where later cards are far below the fold), remove the misleading unused `stagger` prop from RevealGroup's signature entirely and codify `delay={i * 0.06}` as a documented convention (e.g. a shared `STAGGER_STEP` constant) instead of three different hand-typed magic numbers.

findings.title: No route-level loading.tsx / Suspense fallback anywhere in the app, ahead of the spec's own planned CMS migration
findings.area: src/app/[locale]/** (glob for loading.tsx returned zero matches)
findings.evidence: A glob for `src/app/[locale]/**/loading.tsx` across the entire route tree returns no results, and no manual `<Suspense>` boundaries were found wrapping async segments. Today this is largely masked because content is read from local, synchronous JSON via typed getters (PROJECT_SPEC.md Section 4.1), so most navigations resolve fast even without a fallback UI. But Section 4.1 explicitly documents a planned migration to a hosted Sanity CMS where 'only the data-fetching functions change' — once that lands, route segments will perform real network-latency data fetches with the exact same zero-fallback-UI structure that exists today, producing a blank gap on slower connections (a real condition for Gulf-region mobile users on hospital/enterprise networks) instead of a skeleton.
findings.recommendation: Add at least a shared `loading.tsx` pattern (even a simple skeleton matching the page's grid/card shapes) for the higher-traffic dynamic segments (products/[slug], solutions/[slug], partners/[slug], knowledge-center/[slug]) now, while it's cheap, rather than retrofitting it at the same time as the CMS migration when there will be more surface area to cover.

findings.title: useReducedMotion() is read synchronously at render time, not effect-gated — theoretical hydration-mismatch risk for the specific users the feature is meant to protect
findings.area: node_modules/framer-motion/dist/es/utils/reduced-motion/use-reduced-motion.mjs (library internal, consumed by src/components/motion/reveal.tsx:21 and src/components/ui/stat-counter.tsx:23)
findings.evidence: framer-motion's useReducedMotion lazily initializes `prefersReducedMotion.current` via `window.matchMedia` synchronously during the component's render pass (not inside a useEffect) — `!hasReducedMotionListener.current && initPrefersReducedMotion()` runs unconditionally at the top of the hook body. Because Reveal/StatCounter are client components rendered inside a server-rendered tree, the server has no `window` and presumably renders assuming no reduced-motion preference, while the client's very first render pass reads the real OS setting synchronously (not deferred to an effect the way most SSR-safe media-query hooks are written) — creating a possible attribute/style mismatch specifically for the subset of visitors who have OS-level 'reduce motion' enabled, i.e. exactly the accessibility-conscious users this code path exists to serve correctly.
findings.recommendation: This is a third-party library implementation detail, not something to patch directly, but worth a quick manual check (DevTools 'Emulate CSS prefers-reduced-motion: reduce' + hard reload on a Reveal-heavy page, watching the console for hydration-mismatch warnings) to confirm whether it's purely theoretical here or produces a visible flash/warning in practice; if it does, wrapping the site's own `hidden` variant selection in a `useEffect`-confirmed value (mirroring the pattern StatCounter already half-does with its `useState(shouldReduceMotion ? value : 0)` initializer) would close the gap without touching the library.

reports.lens: UX / Usability Heuristics — Information Architecture, Navigation, Forms, and Lead-Gen Funnel
reports.summary: The site's IA is sound and its accessibility engineering for forms is genuinely above average (aria-invalid/aria-describedby/role=alert wiring, RTL-aware breadcrumbs with JSON-LD, thoughtful query-param inquiry-type prefill from Services to Contact). But the lead-gen funnel — the site's whole reason for existing — has real friction and consistency problems: the two primary conversion modals (Demo Request, Quotation Request) are dense 8-9-field single-screen forms that are meaningfully heavier than the site's own general Contact form, every button in the design system (including the "lg" CTA variant) renders below the accepted 44px touch-target minimum, the header's primary "Request a Demo" CTA disappears entirely below the sm breakpoint with no replacement inside the mobile hamburger menu, the Services page — arguably the page carrying the "partner not distributor" positioning — ends in the weakest-looking CTA on the site (a small underlined text link) while every other detail page ends in a bold gradient CTA band, and the confirmed site-wide scroll-reveal bug means a visitor who lands on the Home hero or the Contact page and doesn't immediately scroll may stare at a near-invisible headline, CTA buttons, or form for several seconds. None of these individually block conversion, but stacked together they add friction at exactly the moments that matter most for a B2B procurement buyer deciding whether to hand over their details.
strengths: Form accessibility is well engineered, not an afterthought: src/components/ui/form-field.tsx clones aria-invalid + aria-describedby onto the input and renders role="alert" error text, so both first-appearance screen-reader announcement and re-focus-on-invalid-field are covered — a level of care most B2B sites skip.

Desktop nav mega-menus for Solutions and Partners (src/components/layout/desktop-nav.tsx) correctly reduce a large sitemap to a manageable top-level count while still surfacing all 5 clinical categories and 4 partners one hover away, with a 'View all' escape hatch in each panel.

The Services page CTA -> Contact page prefill (src/app/[locale]/contact/page.tsx lines 14-22) is genuinely thoughtful funnel engineering: each service card's CTA passes a ?type= param that maps onto the Contact form's inquiry-type selector, including a documented fallback for 'tender-support' -> 'sales' since Contact's schema has no literal match — so a hospital buyer coming from 'Maintenance & Preventive Maintenance' lands on a form already routed correctly instead of a generic blank one.

The Contact form itself (src/components/sections/contact/contact-form.tsx) is appropriately lightweight for a general inquiry — inquiry type, name, email, phone, message, with organization optional — the right friction level for a first-touch B2B contact form.

Breadcrumbs (src/components/layout/page-breadcrumb.tsx) are implemented correctly for RTL (chevron mirrors via rtl:rotate-180), emit BreadcrumbList JSON-LD from the same trail data every interior page already provides, and use a semantic ol/li structure via Fragment rather than a div/span that would fail axe's list-child check.

CtaBand (src/components/sections/cta-band.tsx) is consistently wired into every detail-page type that should end in conversion — Products, Solutions, Partners, and Knowledge Center articles all end in a QuotationRequestModal + Contact button pairing — so the 'never end in nothing' rule the business brief implies is followed for the site's main content types.

findings.title: Primary 'Request a Demo' CTA vanishes on mobile with no replacement in the hamburger menu
findings.evidence: src/components/layout/header.tsx lines 55-57 wrap the header's DemoRequestModal in `<div className="hidden sm:block">`, so it does not render at all below the sm breakpoint (~640px, i.e. phones). src/components/layout/mobile-nav.tsx (the hamburger Sheet, lines 43-98) lists Home, the Solutions/Partners accordions, and the rest of primaryNav — it contains no Demo/Quotation CTA anywhere. A phone visitor therefore has zero header-level access to the site's flagship lead-gen action; they must first navigate into a specific detail page to find a CtaBand.
findings.recommendation: Either show a compact icon-only DemoRequestModal trigger next to the hamburger icon at all widths, or add a persistent 'Request a Demo' action inside the MobileNav Sheet itself so mobile users always have one tap to the CTA.
findings.industry_rationale: Procurement and biomedical-engineering contacts frequently first encounter a vendor site via a shared link opened on a phone (WhatsApp forward, email on mobile). Losing the header CTA on exactly that device class removes the lowest-friction conversion path for a segment that is disproportionately likely to be time-boxed and not inclined to hunt through subpages.

findings.title: Site-wide scroll-reveal bug hits the two highest-value moments in the funnel: the Home hero CTA and the Contact form
findings.evidence: src/components/motion/reveal.tsx (Reveal, lines 29-40; RevealGroup, lines 54-66) uses framer-motion whileInView with viewport={{ once: true, margin: "-80px" }} and no fallback for the confirmed case where the IntersectionObserver-backed check does not fire reliably on mount. src/components/sections/home/hero.tsx wraps the H1/subhead in Reveal (line 25) and the primary CTA row — Button('Explore Solutions') + DemoRequestModal — in a second Reveal with delay=0.16 (lines 38-45), i.e. exactly the content a first-time visitor needs to read and act on before scrolling. src/app/[locale]/contact/page.tsx wraps the entire ContactForm in one Reveal (line 78) and the phone/email/map sidebar in another (line 82) — the bottom-of-funnel form itself is gated behind the same unreliable animation.
findings.recommendation: Given this is already confirmed live, treat it as the top fix priority ahead of other UX polish: add an explicit fallback (e.g. force visible after a short mount timeout, or switch above-the-fold hero/CTA content and the Contact form to animate on mount rather than on whileInView) so first-paint content is never gated behind a scroll gesture.
findings.industry_rationale: A Ministry of Health or hospital-administrator visitor who lands on the homepage and reads the hero before scrolling — the default reading behavior for a hero — may see a blank area where the headline and 'Request a Demo' button should be. The same failure mode hits someone who clicks straight through to Contact intending to fill the form immediately. Neither user is doing anything unusual; the site is failing its most common, most valuable interaction pattern.

findings.title: Every button in the design system, including the site's primary CTAs, renders under the 44px touch-target minimum
findings.evidence: src/components/ui/button.tsx size variants: default h-8 (32px), sm h-7 (28px), lg h-9 (36px), icon size-8 (32px) — the largest available non-icon size ('lg') is still 8px short of the 44px baseline. DemoRequestModal and QuotationRequestModal both default to size="sm" (28px tall) when no size prop is passed (demo-request-modal.tsx line 39, quotation-request-modal.tsx line 39); the header's DemoRequestModal (header.tsx line 56) uses this default, so the single most-repeated CTA in the entire site is a 28px-tall tap target.
findings.recommendation: Raise the 'lg' variant to at least h-11 (44px) and use it as the mandatory size for every Demo/Quotation/Contact CTA trigger sitewide, including the header default; reserve the smaller sizes for dense in-page utility controls (table actions, filter chips), not for lead-gen CTAs.
findings.industry_rationale: The stated audience includes hospital administrators and biomedical engineers who plausibly browse supplier sites on tablets/phones between meetings or on hospital floors; undersized primary CTAs increase mis-taps and abandoned interactions specifically at the conversion moment, and read as unpolished next to the Medtronic/Stryker/GE-tier visual bar the brief targets — those sites consistently use generously-sized primary buttons.

findings.title: Demo Request and Quotation Request modals demand 8-9 required fields in a single unstepped screen — heavier than the site's own general Contact form
findings.area: Demo Request modal / Quotation Request modal
findings.evidence: demo-request-modal.tsx requires fullName, organization, jobTitle, department, city, email, mobile, preferredContactMethod, and productOrSolutionOfInterest — 9 required fields (validations/leads.ts lines 20-31), all presented at once in a 2-column grid inside a Dialog capped at max-h-[85vh] with internal overflow-y-auto (line 100). quotation-request-modal.tsx requires organization, contactPerson, department, product, quantity, city, and procurementType — 7 required fields (validations/leads.ts lines 34-44). By contrast the general ContactForm (contact-form.tsx) requires only inquiryType, name, email, phone, and message, with organization optional. The two CTAs styled as the site's fastest 'quick action', triggered directly from every header and every detail-page CTA band, are the two forms with the most friction.
findings.recommendation: Cut the Demo Request modal to the essentials for a first touch (name, organization, email, mobile, product/solution of interest) and move job title, department, city, and preferred contact method to either an optional 'tell us more' expandable section or a follow-up step after submission. Alternatively, convert both modals into a genuine 2-step flow (contact basics -> optional qualifying detail) so the form actually matches the multi-step pattern its field count implies, with visible step progress.
findings.industry_rationale: For a B2B lead-gen site the first-touch CTA ('Request a Demo' clicked from a hero or nav) should be the lowest-friction entry point, with qualifying detail (department, job title, procurement type) deferred to a follow-up call or a secondary step — standard practice on the Medtronic/Stryker-tier sites the brief cites as the bar. Asking for job title, department, city, and preferred contact method before a prospect has even spoken to a human is a well-documented conversion killer, and it's inconsistent that the site's own lighter-weight Contact form contradicts the modals' assumption that this much detail is needed upfront.

findings.title: Services page — the page carrying the 'technology partner, not distributor' positioning — ends in the weakest CTA treatment on the site
findings.evidence: src/app/[locale]/services/page.tsx lines 72-79: each service card's call to action is a plain inline text link — `<Link ... className="mt-4 text-sm font-medium text-emc-teal-700 hover:underline">{t("cta.contactEmc")}</Link>` — rendered only conditionally (`service.ctaType &&`), with no button chrome, inside a card that otherwise looks identical to a static content tile. Every other detail-page type (Products, Solutions, Partners, Knowledge Center — confirmed via grep for CtaBand usage across src/app) ends in the bold gradient CtaBand with a full-size button pair.
findings.recommendation: Give each service card (or the page as a whole) a real button-styled CTA consistent with CtaBand's visual weight, and consider adding a page-level CtaBand at the bottom of Services (as exists on every other listing-to-detail content type) rather than relying solely on per-card text links.
findings.industry_rationale: Per the brief, Services (Clinical Training, Hands-on Workshops, Installation, Commissioning, Maintenance & PM) is the primary evidence that EMC is a technology partner rather than a distributor reselling a supplier-logo grid — exactly the content that should convert hardest, not softest. A low-contrast text link is easy to miss when scanning a 3-column grid and undersells the differentiator the whole rebuild is built around.

findings.title: Footer omits the Partners section entirely
findings.evidence: src/components/layout/footer.tsx lines 55-74: the 'Quick Links' column maps over `primaryNav` (Home, Products, Services, Knowledge Center, About, Careers, Contact) and then manually appends one extra link for `solutionsMenu.href` (lines 66-73). `partnersMenu.href` (/partners) is never added anywhere in the footer, even though partnersMenu is imported and used elsewhere in the codebase. Partners is reachable only from the top nav mega-menu or a deep link.
findings.recommendation: Add a link to `partnersMenu.href` in the footer's Quick Links list alongside the Solutions link that's already there.
findings.industry_rationale: The footer is the fallback navigation surface users check when they've scrolled past the header and want an overview of everything the site offers; for a credibility-driven B2B site, 'who are your partners' (UE Medical, Long Life Surgical, AMECO) is exactly the kind of institutional-trust content a buyer scans the footer for. Its absence is a small but real findability gap, and looks like an oversight next to Solutions being explicitly added there.

findings.title: Header search affordance is a non-functional decoy — opens a permanently disabled input labeled 'coming soon'
findings.evidence: src/components/layout/search-trigger.tsx: the search icon opens a Popover containing `<Input type="search" ... disabled />` and a 'comingSoon' caption (lines 27-35). The component's own comment confirms this is intentional: 'UI shell only in Phase 1 — the Fuse.js index has nothing to index until Phases 2-4 ship content.' It is nonetheless live in the shipped header on every page.
findings.recommendation: Either finish and ship the Fuse.js-backed search before this reaches production traffic, or remove the search icon entirely until it's functional — a missing feature reads better than a visibly broken one.
findings.industry_rationale: A technical procurement buyer looking for a specific product/model number will reasonably expect the visible magnifying-glass icon in the header to search the catalog — that's the universal convention. Discovering it's inert breaks the 'system does what it visibly offers' heuristic, and for an audience evaluating whether this vendor is operationally mature enough to trust with equipment procurement, an obviously half-shipped feature undercuts the credibility goal stated in the brief.

findings.title: Demo/Quotation modal dialogs risk double-scrolling on small/short viewports (page scroll + internal modal scroll)
findings.area: Demo Request modal / Quotation Request modal (layout; not yet verified live on mobile)
findings.evidence: Both modals set `className="max-h-[85vh] overflow-y-auto sm:max-w-lg"` on DialogContent (demo-request-modal.tsx line 100, quotation-request-modal.tsx line 102) around an 8-9 field 2-column grid. On a short mobile viewport (e.g. an iPhone SE at ~667px tall, or any device with the on-screen keyboard open, which shrinks usable viewport height further), 85vh leaves very little room, and a fixed dialog header plus a separately-scrollable field list inside a modal is a known-awkward interaction pattern.
findings.recommendation: Flagged as an open verification item per the review brief — confirm real behavior on a narrow/short viewport with the keyboard open before or shortly after launch; shortening the required-field count (see the field-count finding above) will materially reduce the severity of this regardless.
findings.industry_rationale: This compounds the field-count finding above: a long form crammed into a capped-height modal on a small screen, with the keyboard open, is one of the more failure-prone form-entry contexts for exactly the mobile procurement-buyer segment this audit is concerned about.

findings.title: Gradient-blob placeholder stands in for editorial photography on every high-intent detail page
findings.area: Solution/Product/Partner detail pages, About page (GradientMesh component)
findings.evidence: src/components/sections/gradient-mesh.tsx renders a purple/teal radial-gradient panel with a faint grid overlay, and its own code comment states it is a 'stand-in for editorial photography (none supplied yet)'. It is wired into src/app/[locale]/about/page.tsx:58, src/app/[locale]/solutions/[slug]/page.tsx:115, src/app/[locale]/products/[slug]/page.tsx:136, and src/app/[locale]/partners/[slug]/page.tsx:125-129 — i.e. the About hero and every Solution, Product, and Partner detail page. Screenshots 4 and 8 (About hero, Anesthesia & Airway Management hero) confirm it renders as a generic abstract gradient, not a device or clinical photo. Screenshot 5 (Products listing) shows real editorial medical-device photography exists and is used elsewhere on the site, so the contrast is visible within a single browsing session.
findings.recommendation: Treat this as a pre-launch blocker, not a style choice: source or commission real photography/product renders for every solution, product, and partner detail page before launch. Until assets exist, do not ship the placeholder to a page a buyer can reach in normal navigation — either gate those routes or use a visibly-labeled temporary state, because right now it reads as an unfinished build, not a restrained design decision.
findings.industry_rationale: The stated bar is explicitly 'Medtronic, Stryker, GE Healthcare, Philips... large editorial photography.' A biomedical engineer or procurement officer clicking from a photographed product card into that product's own detail page and hitting a generic purple/teal blob instead of the device reads as unfinished or low-budget — the opposite of the 'global technology partner' repositioning the rebuild is trying to achieve, and it happens on exactly the pages where a credentialed buyer is deciding whether to trust the vendor.

findings.title: One repeated icon-chip card template carries nearly every section on the site
findings.area: Solutions grid, Products grid, About pillars/values, Services listing, Solution/Product detail heroes, desktop nav dropdown
findings.evidence: grep across src confirms the identical `inline-flex size-11 items-center justify-center rounded-xl bg-emc-teal-100 text-emc-purple-700` icon chip (generic Lucide icon via DynamicIcon) appears in solution-card.tsx, product-card.tsx, about/pillar-card.tsx, solutions/[slug]/page.tsx:86, services/page.tsx:63, and desktop-nav.tsx:80. Screenshots 2 and 6 show the same icon-in-square + heading + one-line description + 'Learn more' unit repeated 5x on Solutions and 3x visible on Home for entirely different clinical categories (a syringe icon for Anesthesia, a heart for Critical Care, a truck for Emergency).
findings.recommendation: Reserve the icon-chip pattern for one or two content types (e.g. Services) and differentiate the higher-stakes category — Solutions — with actual imagery or a distinct, more editorial treatment per category, since these are the site's core navigational taxonomy, not interchangeable feature bullets.
findings.industry_rationale: This is the impeccable design system's own named anti-pattern ('large rounded-corner icons above every heading... screams template'; 'identical card grids... repeated endlessly'). Generic off-the-shelf Lucide pictograms standing in for five distinct clinical categories (anesthesia, critical care, emergency, nursing, respiratory) read as a stock SaaS template, not as a specialist medical-technology partner with category-specific expertise — the opposite signal from Medtronic/Stryker-style category pages, which lean on photography and purpose-built iconography.

findings.title: Card grammar is inconsistent within a single page and a single user journey
findings.evidence: src/app/[locale]/solutions/[slug]/page.tsx lines 139-153: the related-Partners cards on a Solution detail page are plain `rounded-2xl border border-border bg-card p-6` boxes with no icon, logo, or photo — a visibly different 'species' of card from the icon-chip Solution cards on Home/Solutions listing and the icon-chip Product cards two sections below on the same page. Screenshot 3 confirms three bare white cards with only a heading, a paragraph, and a text link.
findings.recommendation: Give the Partners cross-sell cards the partner's logo (already built for the Partners index via PartnerTile's logo-with-wordmark-fallback pattern) rather than a bare bordered box, so the same content type looks the same wherever it appears.
findings.industry_rationale: A procurement or biomedical audience is scanning for signals of who actually backs a product (UE Medical, Long Life, AMECO). A flat, iconless, logo-less card for the partner relationship — arguably the most credibility-bearing content on the page — undersells it relative to the more visually resolved Solution and Product cards immediately above and below it.

findings.title: About page uses brand purple as a repeated full-bleed background, not an accent
findings.evidence: globals.css:97 documents the rule explicitly: 'Surfaces are white/soft-gray dominant; purple and teal are accents only.' On the About page alone, solid `bg-emc-purple-900` is used three times as a background field: the GradientMesh hero (line 58), the 'Vision' card (line 80), and the full-width 'Corporate Philosophy' band (line 162) — confirmed by grep. Screenshot 4 shows the hero already committing a large purple/teal panel; two more purple-900 blocks follow further down the same page.
findings.recommendation: Keep one deliberate purple field per page (the hero, once real photography replaces it, or the closing CTA), and restyle the Vision card and Corporate Philosophy band with the neutral/teal-accent treatment used elsewhere (e.g. the Mission card's white-with-border style) so purple reads as a single intentional beat, not the page's default surface.
findings.industry_rationale: The team has clearly already done deliberate, documented contrast-ratio work to keep purple/teal disciplined as accents (see the WCAG comments in globals.css) — this finding is about a page that drifts from that self-imposed rule, undermining the 'restrained' half of the stated Medtronic/Stryker/Philips bar specifically on the page (About) most responsible for establishing institutional credibility.

findings.title: The confirmed Reveal opacity bug has a visible, compounding cosmetic failure mode on placeholder-hero pages
