findings.evidence: Screenshot 8 (Anesthesia & Airway Management hero) appears to have been captured while affected: the h1, subhead, and both CTA buttons ('Speak with a Product Specialist', 'Request a Demo') render at near-zero opacity, and the GradientMesh panel that should sit beside them is not visible either, leaving a mostly blank white viewport below the nav. This is downstream of the already-confirmed reveal.tsx bug, not a new defect, but the visual-craft consequence is worth naming: it compounds with Finding 1 (placeholder hero art) so a visitor who lands without immediately scrolling may see an apparently empty, broken page rather than a specialist's confident hero.
findings.recommendation: No new fix needed beyond resolving the underlying reveal.tsx issue already flagged; treat the fix as higher priority given this visible interaction with the hero-imagery gap, since together they can produce a near-blank first impression on a solution page.
findings.industry_rationale: For a lead-generation site where the hero and its CTA are the primary conversion surface, several seconds of an apparently blank page on first load is a direct hit to the 'confident, precise' impression the brief asks for, and is more damaging on a Solution/Product page (where the visitor already has high purchase intent) than on a page with lower stakes.

findings.title: Primary CTA buttons are cramped relative to the enterprise visual weight the brief asks for
findings.evidence: The 'lg' size variant used for every primary hero/CTA button site-wide (Home hero, Solution/Product detail heroes, CTA bands) is `h-9 gap-1.5 px-2.5` — 36px tall with only 10px of horizontal padding per side. There is no larger button size in the scale at all (default h-8/32px, lg h-9/36px, sizes otherwise only vary for icon buttons).
findings.recommendation: Add a genuinely larger CTA size (e.g. h-11/44px with px-5/20px+ horizontal padding) reserved for hero and CTA-band primary actions, distinct from the compact 'lg' used for in-page secondary actions like nav buttons.
findings.industry_rationale: Medtronic/Stryker/Philips-tier marketing sites give primary conversion actions (the exact 'Request a Demo' / 'Request a Quotation' buttons this rebuild is built around) more visual weight than a 36px chip-sized button; undersized CTAs read as an app control, not a considered invitation to a procurement contact.

strengths: Color-token discipline is genuinely deliberate, not just aesthetic: globals.css documents a specific teal-700-for-text vs teal-600-for-icons split, with inline WCAG contrast-ratio math explaining why (teal-600 measures 3.66:1 on white and fails AA for text; teal-700 clears 4.9:1). This is real craft rigor that most B2B rebuilds skip.

Section vertical rhythm is consistently disciplined: the large majority of section wrappers across Home, About, Solutions, Products, and Partners use the same py-16 sm:py-24 pairing (confirmed via grep across 9+ section files), with legible, purposeful exceptions — trust-band at py-8 for a thin strip, stats-band at py-16 sm:py-20 for a denser navy band — rather than arbitrary one-off spacing per section.

Honesty-over-fabrication is built into the components themselves: testimonials-section.tsx explicitly returns null rather than render placeholder/mock testimonials, and partner-tile.tsx falls back to a clean wordmark treatment instead of fabricating a partner logo. For a credibility-first procurement audience, refusing to fake content is itself a polish signal worth protecting as real assets land.

Typographic hierarchy differentiates the home page from interior pages on purpose: the Home hero h1 scales up to text-6xl at large breakpoints while every interior-page h1 (About, Solutions, Products, Partners, Solution/Product detail) caps at text-5xl, giving the homepage more visual weight without inflating the whole site's scale into flatness.

Interactive states are applied uniformly wherever cards do appear: the same hover (-translate-y-1, shadow-lg) and focus-visible outline treatment is used consistently across solution, product, and partner tiles, so even where card content itself is repetitive, the interaction feel is coherent sitewide.

The Home hero itself (screenshot 1) is a strong, on-brief exemplar of the stated bar: real editorial surgical-team photography, generous whitespace, a restrained teal eyebrow label, and a single purple primary CTA — proof the team can hit the Medtronic/Stryker register when real photography exists.
reports.summary: The site clearly has real design-system discipline underneath it — documented WCAG-driven color tokens, consistent section spacing rhythm, and a refusal to fabricate testimonials or logos — and the Home hero shows the team can hit the stated Medtronic/Stryker/Philips bar when real photography is in hand. But that discipline breaks down in two compounding ways once you leave the homepage: first, a single reused 'icon-in-teal-square + heading + one-liner' card template (the shared design law's own named anti-pattern) carries almost every section on the site, making five clinically distinct solution categories look interchangeable; second, and more seriously, the GradientMesh abstract purple/teal blob is hard-coded (by its own code comment) as a photography placeholder across every Solution, Product, and Partner detail page plus the About hero — exactly the pages where a procurement or biomedical buyer is closest to a decision, and exactly where the brief's 'large editorial photography' promise is least fulfilled. Layered with the already-confirmed Reveal opacity bug, a solution-page hero can currently present as a near-blank viewport with no photography, no visible headline, and no visible CTA. The gap between the site's evident capability (Home hero, token discipline, spacing rhythm) and its weakest surfaces (detail-page heroes, repeated card template) is the story here, not a uniform lack of craft."

reports.lens: Premium editorial visual system fit (bar: Medtronic / Stryker / GE Healthcare / Philips Healthcare / Karl Storz / Drager)
reports.summary: The design SYSTEM (color tokens, spacing scale, restrained-accent rule, motion primitives) is genuinely disciplined and, on the one page that has real assets to work with — Home — it clears the stated bar: large editorial photography, generous white space, purple/teal used only as accents. But the moment a visitor leaves Home, the site runs out of photography. Total real photographic assets in the entire codebase are six files (public/media/photos has exactly 2 generic stock-style photos, both used only on Home; public/media/products has 4 product shots for the site's only 3 SKUs). Every other page that is supposed to do the 'credibility partner, not distributor' storytelling work — About, all 5 Solution detail pages, Product detail, Partner detail — substitutes a flat purple/teal gradient block (src/components/sections/gradient-mesh.tsx, literally commented 'Stand-in for editorial photography (none supplied yet)') where Medtronic/Stryker would run a large OR or device-in-use photograph. Layered on top of that is a confirmed live bug (src/components/motion/reveal.tsx) that leaves hero and body text at near-zero opacity for several seconds on page load, so even the one page that does have photography can present as broken before a visitor scrolls. Net effect: Home reads as premium; every interior page currently reads as an unfinished template wearing the right color palette, and the Partners/Solutions listing pages still lean on logo-and-card patterns that are structurally the 'regional distributor catalog' the brief explicitly wants to move away from, just with better copy than before.
strengths: Home hero (screenshot: home hero) genuinely hits the stated bar — large real photography (surgical team, natural composition) at roughly half the viewport, teal eyebrow + purple CTA as the only saturated color, generous padding (py-16/py-24 scale in hero.tsx). This is the strongest single screen in the site and is a legitimate reference for what the rest of the site should look like.

src/app/globals.css documents a real, defensible color-contrast decision (teal-700 vs teal-600, ring color) with WCAG ratios inline in comments — this is unusual engineering rigor for a marketing site and directly supports the 'confident, precise, evidence-oriented' tone the brief wants from the brand itself, not just the copy.

The purple/teal-as-accent rule from Section 6.1 of PROJECT_SPEC.md is actually enforced in the token architecture (--background/--card/--muted all map to white/soft-gray; --primary/--secondary/--accent are the only purple/teal touchpoints) — this is the correct foundation for the Medtronic/Stryker look even though most pages aren't yet populated enough to show it off.

CustomerMarquee (src/components/sections/home/customer-marquee.tsx) is a restrained, well-engineered logo band: pauses on hover/focus, respects prefers-reduced-motion by falling back to a static wrap, supports drag/wheel — it's a 'trusted by' pattern used by every reference brand in the bar, executed without gimmick.

The team's discipline against fabricating stats/testimonials (verified:false gating documented in PROJECT_SPEC.md Section 8) is itself a premium-B2B-trust signal once photography catches up — GE Healthcare and Philips also avoid inflated claims in favor of specific, sourced facts, which is the posture this codebase is built to support.

Products and Solutions listing pages (screenshots 5 and 6) have real editorial breathing room — wide margins, a single confident H1, muted subhead, and search/filter controls that don't crowd the fold. The layout skeleton is right even where the content inside it (photography, catalog depth) isn't there yet.

findings.title: Scroll-reveal bug makes hero and body copy invisible on load sitewide, undermining the one thing the design system does well
findings.area: Sitewide — Home, About, Products, Solutions listing, Solution detail, Contact (all confirmed affected per session notes)
findings.evidence: src/components/motion/reveal.tsx: Reveal/RevealGroup use framer-motion whileInView with viewport={{ once: true, margin: '-80px' }} (lines 34, 59); the IntersectionObserver check does not reliably fire on initial mount, so wrapped content sits at opacity:0 (variants line 25) until any scroll gesture. Screenshot 8 (Anesthesia & Airway Management solution detail hero) shows this live: the H1, subhead, and both CTA buttons are rendered at near-zero opacity with no user action taken yet.
findings.recommendation: Treat as a P0 fix, not a polish item: switch the mount-time reveal to either (a) an `animate` state gated on a mounted flag with a hard fallback to visible after a short timeout, or (b) skip whileInView entirely for above-the-fold content on first paint (only animate on subsequent client-side nav) so a hero headline is never the thing at risk of being invisible.
findings.industry_rationale: A MOH/NUPCO procurement reviewer or hospital administrator who lands on a page and reads before scrolling — the single most common way to read a hero headline — may see a blank page. For a site whose entire job is to read as credible and finished to a skeptical institutional buyer, an apparently-broken hero is a worse first impression than plain, unanimated text would be; it reads as 'unfinished vendor site,' which is the exact opposite of the positioning goal.

findings.title: Zero real photography on every page except Home — interior pages substitute a flat gradient block where the bar demands large editorial imagery
findings.area: About, all 5 Solution detail pages, Product detail, Partner detail (src/components/sections/gradient-mesh.tsx, used in about/page.tsx, solutions/[slug]/page.tsx, products/[slug]/page.tsx, partners/[slug]/page.tsx)
findings.evidence: public/media/photos/ contains exactly 2 files total (1.jpeg, 2.jpeg), both used only on Home (hero.tsx line 50, featured-technology.tsx line 29 — the second one is object-contain with padding, i.e. a product-on-white shot, not an editorial scene). Every other detail-page hero renders GradientMesh instead: a component whose own code comment reads 'Stand-in for editorial photography (none supplied yet — Section 15 only provides the logo raster and the UE Medical PDF).' Screenshot 4 (About hero) and screenshot 8 (Anesthesia solution hero) both confirm this live — a purple/teal radial gradient with a faint grid-line texture sits where a Stryker or Medtronic page would run a large clinical photograph.
findings.recommendation: Prioritize sourcing/commissioning real photography for About and the 5 Solution detail heroes before anything else visual — these are the pages doing the 'healthcare technology partner' persuasion work, not Home. Until real photography exists, consider a less generic interim treatment (e.g., a duotone-treated stock clinical photo licensed short-term, or the existing 2 photos reused with different crops/duotone per section) rather than a flat gradient, which reads as a design-system placeholder to any visitor, not as an intentional brand choice.
findings.industry_rationale: The stated bar names photography usage first ('large editorial photography'). None of Medtronic, Stryker, GE Healthcare, Philips, Karl Storz, or Drager ship a solution or about page without a hero photograph of a device, a clinician, or a care setting — it's the primary way those brands establish clinical credibility non-verbally. A gradient block in that slot is legible as 'photography not supplied yet' to any visitor who has seen a competitor's site, which is precisely the audience (biomedical engineers, procurement, clinical consultants) evaluating EMC against those brands.

findings.title: Product catalog and photography depth is too thin to read as a real catalog yet
findings.evidence: content/products/ contains only 3 product JSON files (uescope-video-laryngoscope, sacovlm-video-laryngeal-mask, flexible-bronchoscope); all 3 happen to have heroImage set, but ProductCard.tsx (lines 25-41) falls back to a small teal-tinted icon square whenever heroImage is absent — the pattern used sitewide for anything not yet photographed.
findings.recommendation: Either gate the Products nav item/page behind having a critical mass of SKUs with real photography, or explicitly frame the current 3 as 'Featured Products' rather than 'Browse Our Products' (screenshot 5 headline) so a 3-item result set doesn't read as the entire catalog. As more SKUs are added, photography must be sourced per-product before publishing — the icon fallback should be treated as a content gap indicator, not a shippable end state.
findings.industry_rationale: GE Healthcare and Philips product pages never fall back to a generic pictogram — absence of a device photo on a device page reads as 'this isn't a real inventory item' to a biomedical engineer or procurement contact doing due diligence, undermining the credibility goal more than simply having fewer, fully-photographed products would.

findings.title: Partners section is still a logo-plus-paragraph card grid, not photography-led partner storytelling
findings.area: Partners listing (screenshot: partners listing / solution detail bottom cross-sell), src/components/sections/home/partners-band.tsx, src/components/sections/partner-tile.tsx
findings.evidence: Screenshot 3 shows the Partners section as three bordered white cards, each with a small wordmark, 2-3 sentences of (well-written, factual) company history, and a 'Learn more' link — no imagery of the partner's manufacturing facility, product line, or a UE Medical/Long Life device in use. PartnersBand (home/partners-band.tsx) renders the same PartnerTile pattern on Home.
findings.recommendation: Once partner-supplied imagery exists (facility photos, hero device shots, UE Medical's own presentation deck referenced in PROJECT_SPEC.md likely has usable stills), replace the card-grid with a photography-led module per partner — large image + shorter copy — reserving the current card format for a secondary/index view only.
findings.industry_rationale: This is the literal pattern named in the brief as the thing to move away from — 'a regional distributor with a supplier-logo grid.' The copy has been rewritten to be specific and credible (verified founding dates, ISO certifications), which is real progress, but the visual container is unchanged from a standard distributor partner-list template, so the positioning shift is currently legible in the words but not yet in the layout.

findings.title: Icon system on Solutions/Products listing is generic and interchangeable, not distinctive enough to carry pages that lack photography
findings.area: Solutions listing/detail, Products fallback (screenshot: solutions listing, home mid-scroll clinical categories grid)
findings.evidence: Screenshots 2 and 6 show 5 solution cards distinguished only by a small line icon (syringe, heart, ambulance, keyboard/monitor, lungs) in a teal-100 rounded square — otherwise identical white bordered cards with the same type scale and 'Learn more' link treatment.
findings.recommendation: These icon+card grids are an acceptable index/overview pattern (Home mid-scroll works fine as a scanning aid), but they should not be the primary visual identity carrier for a clinical category — once solution-detail photography lands, consider pulling a representative photo crop into the listing cards too, reserving pure icon grids for secondary navigation only.
findings.industry_rationale: None of the six reference brands rely on generic line-icon grids to differentiate clinical categories at this level of the site hierarchy — icons appear as secondary wayfinding, with photography or bold typographic treatment carrying primary differentiation. Right now this grid could belong to almost any medical-supply company's site, which cuts against 'premium healthcare technology partner' distinctiveness.

findings.title: Interior-page 'white space' currently reads as unfinished placeholder rather than intentional restraint
findings.evidence: The About and Solution-detail heroes pair a left column of text with a large (roughly 640x460px in screenshot 4) flat gradient rectangle on the right — visually this occupies the same footprint 'generous white space' would, but reads as an empty box rather than breathing room because it's a placeholder component, not a deliberate compositional choice.
findings.recommendation: No action needed beyond fixing finding #2 (real photography) — flagging this only so the team doesn't mistake the current interior-page emptiness for the 'generous white space' the brief calls for; the two are visually similar but read very differently to a visitor once they notice the pattern repeats identically across five different solution categories.
findings.industry_rationale: Generous white space is a deliberate compositional choice around content that is present; an empty placeholder in the same footprint reads as absence, not restraint, once a visitor recognizes the same block repeating on every category page.

findings.title: Mobile rendering of the photography/reveal issues not verified this session
findings.evidence: Per session constraints, the browser tool could not reliably render below desktop width, so how GradientMesh, the aspect-ratio hero image containers (aspect-[4/3]/aspect-square in hero.tsx), and the Reveal viewport margin (-80px) behave on a phone-sized viewport is unconfirmed.
findings.recommendation: Before shipping fixes for findings #1 and #2, re-verify on an actual small viewport — a -80px intersection margin and a stuck-at-opacity-0 bug could behave differently (better or worse) when the hero image collapses above the fold on mobile, and that is where most Gulf-region procurement/clinical traffic on phones will actually experience these pages first.
findings.industry_rationale: Open verification item, not a confirmed defect — flagged per instructions rather than asserted as broken.

reports.summary: This codebase reflects a genuine, above-average accessibility effort for a B2B site of this size: the team has done real contrast-ratio arithmetic (verified independently below and it checks out), shipped a properly-labeled skip link, semantic landmarks, a reduced-motion-aware auto-scrolling marquee that pauses on hover/focus, decorative-vs-meaningful image handling via aria-hidden, and content-level alt text on product photography that actually describes the device per the spec's own instruction. Against that foundation, the confirmed reveal.tsx bug is the single most consequential defect for this lens: it can leave headline text, CTA buttons, and entire contact-form fields at ~opacity:0 while remaining fully focusable, which is a materially different (and more serious) failure mode for a sighted keyboard user than a purely cosmetic animation glitch — they can tab to and even fill in a form field they cannot see. Beyond that, the gaps are concrete and fixable: form submission success states are not announced to assistive technology (fails SC 4.1.3 Status Messages) on all four lead-gen forms, required-field status is conveyed by a colored asterisk alone with no aria-required/required attribute, the language switcher's accessible name doesn't match its visible label (SC 2.5.3), a hardcoded English 'Close' string appears inside Arabic-locale dialogs with no lang annotation (SC 3.1.2), and the back-to-top button stays keyboard-focusable while invisible. None of these are exotic issues — an axe-core/Lighthouse pass plus a screen-reader smoke test of the two modals and the contact form would catch most of them, and given this audience includes MOH/NUPCO procurement contacts for whom a WCAG conformance statement can be a hard tender requirement, closing them before any compliance claim is made is worth prioritizing over polish work.
strengths: globals.css's inline WCAG comments are accurate, not aspirational — independently recomputed: teal-700 on white = 4.91:1 (matches the '4.9:1' claim, clears 4.5:1 body-text AA), teal-600 on white = 3.66:1 (matches the '3.66:1' claim, correctly reserved for icons/large text at the 3:1 threshold, not body copy), teal-400 on white = 2.27:1 (matches exactly, correctly never used as a light-background focus ring). This is real, verified engineering, not a token comment nobody checked.

Focus rings are broadly correct: button.tsx and input.tsx use focus-visible:ring-ring/50 where --ring resolves to teal-700 (4.9:1 against white, comfortably over the 3:1 non-text-contrast minimum in SC 1.4.11), and it's a documented, deliberate choice in the CSS comments.

src/components/ui/form-field.tsx is a well-built accessible form primitive: it clones aria-invalid and aria-describedby onto the child input only when there's an active error, and pairs it with role="alert" on the error text — covering both the 'error just appeared' and 'tab back into an already-invalid field' cases, more thought than most form wrappers put in.

customer-marquee.tsx is a genuinely strong implementation of SC 2.2.2 (Pause, Stop, Hide): it fully disables its requestAnimationFrame loop under prefers-reduced-motion (rendering a static wrapped grid instead), and even in motion mode it pauses on hover/focus/drag and exposes a single keyboard-focusable container with a descriptive aria-label.

Decorative visuals are correctly suppressed from the accessibility tree: gradient-mesh.tsx conditionally sets aria-hidden="true" only when it has no children (i.e., only when it's purely decorative), so the About/Solution-detail gradient hero backgrounds don't get announced as meaningless images.

Product photography alt text is genuinely descriptive per the spec's own instruction to 'describe the device, not just product photo' — e.g. content/products/uescope-video-laryngoscope.json: "UEScope video laryngoscope handle with an integrated monitor showing an endoscopic airway view" — real content discipline, not placeholder text.

html lang and dir are correctly set per-locale in src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx (lang={locale}, dir="rtl" for ar), a working skip-to-content link is present sitewide, and RTL-aware logical Tailwind properties (start-/end- rather than left-/right-) are used consistently in most fixed-position UI (WhatsApp FAB, back-to-top, skip link).

StatCounter correctly jumps straight to the final value under prefers-reduced-motion rather than merely slowing the count animation, and its numeric text (white/70 on navy-900, recomputed at 8.97:1) clears AA with wide margin.

findings.title: Reveal/RevealGroup's stuck-invisible bug leaves interactive elements keyboard-focusable but invisible sitewide
findings.area: src/components/motion/reveal.tsx, consumed by 30 files including hero.tsx, contact/page.tsx, and every solution/product/about page
findings.evidence: Confirmed live: Reveal sets initial={{opacity:0, y:24}} and only flips to visible on a whileInView IntersectionObserver trigger with viewport={{once:true, margin:'-80px'}}, which frequently fails to fire on initial mount until the user scrolls. Framer Motion applies opacity via inline style only — it does not add visibility:hidden, pointer-events:none, or aria-hidden. hero.tsx wraps the h1, subhead, and CTA buttons (including the Request Demo trigger) each in their own Reveal; contact/page.tsx wraps the entire ContactForm (all its labeled inputs) in a single Reveal. A sighted keyboard user who tabs into the page before scrolling — very plausible on a hero, and highly plausible on the Contact page where the natural first action is to tab into the form — can focus, and in the contact-form case even type into, fields rendered at opacity:0 and functionally invisible.
findings.recommendation: Fix the whileInView reliability issue (e.g. fall back to visible after a short timeout, or use IntersectionObserver directly with a fallback for pre-hydration paints), and as a defense-in-depth measure keep pointer-events/focusability tied to the same visible state so an element can never be focused while still at opacity:0.
findings.industry_rationale: For an MOH/NUPCO procurement reviewer or biomedical engineer filling out the Contact form under time pressure, landing on invisible form fields reads as a broken, untrustworthy site — exactly the impression this credibility-driven rebuild is trying to avoid — and a keyboard/low-vision user hitting this on the primary lead-gen form is a directly measurable conversion loss, not just a cosmetic flaw.

findings.title: Form submission success states are not announced to assistive technology (fails SC 4.1.3 Status Messages)
findings.evidence: In all four forms, on successful submission the component conditionally renders a confirmation block (CheckCircle2 icon + t('forms.successTitle') + t('forms.successBody')) with no role="status", role="alert", or aria-live attribute anywhere on the wrapping div — e.g. demo-request-modal.tsx lines 108-113. Compare to the error path, which correctly uses role="alert" (same file, lines 191-195) — the team clearly knows the pattern for errors but didn't apply it to success.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the success confirmation block in role="status" (or aria-live="polite") so screen reader users who submit a Request Demo, Request Quotation, Contact, or Careers form get a spoken confirmation that the submission succeeded, matching what sighted users see instantly.
findings.industry_rationale: These four forms are the entire lead-generation funnel for the business per the brief. A blind or low-vision procurement contact, biomedical engineer, or job applicant who submits a form and receives no auditory confirmation has no way to know whether their inquiry went through, and may reasonably abandon or duplicate the submission — directly undermining the site's stated core success metric.

findings.title: Required form fields are marked with a colored asterisk only — no aria-required or required attribute
findings.area: src/components/ui/form-field.tsx (renders `{required && *}`), consumed by all lead-gen forms
findings.evidence: Grepped form-field.tsx and src/lib/validations/leads.ts for aria-required/required: no matches anywhere in the codebase. The `required` prop on FormField only conditionally renders a visible `*` glyph; it is never propagated to the underlying Input/Select/Textarea as an HTML required attribute or aria-required="true". Validation is entirely client-side zod on submit (forms use noValidate).
findings.recommendation: Thread the `required` prop through to the wrapped input as `aria-required="true"` (and/or the native `required` attribute) so the requirement is programmatically determinable, not just visually implied by a colored symbol a screen reader may skip or read as a bare 'asterisk'.
findings.industry_rationale: PROJECT_SPEC.md Section 13 sets WCAG 2.1 AA as the explicit bar and calls out 'form errors announced to screen readers' by name — required-field status is the same category of information and the same audience (procurement staff completing a Request Quotation under a tender deadline) benefits from knowing up front, not just after a failed submit, which fields are mandatory.

findings.title: Language switcher's accessible name doesn't match its visible label (fails SC 2.5.3 Label in Name)
findings.evidence: The Link's aria-label is set to t("language") = "Language" (en) / "اللغة" (ar), while the button's visible text content is t("switchLanguage") = "العربية" (en page) / "English" (ar page) — confirmed in messages/en.json lines 157-158 and messages/ar.json lines 157-158. On the English site, a sighted user sees a button labeled 'العربية' but its accessible name announced to screen readers / matched by voice control is just 'Language'.
findings.recommendation: Set aria-label to the same string as the visible text (or omit aria-label entirely and let the accessible name derive from the visible content, which is already unambiguous), so the announced name contains the visible label as required by SC 2.5.3.
findings.industry_rationale: This is a bilingual institutional site where voice-control and screen-reader use by government/hospital staff is plausible; a mismatched accessible name on the one control whose entire job is letting Arabic-preferring users find the language toggle undermines exactly the population most likely to need it.

findings.title: Hardcoded, untranslated 'Close' button text inside dialogs rendered on the Arabic locale
findings.area: src/components/ui/dialog.tsx line 75 (`Close`), affecting all Dialog-based modals sitewide (Demo Request, Quotation Request)
findings.evidence: The sr-only text is a literal English string, not run through next-intl's t(). It renders identically inside Arabic-locale dialogs (html lang="ar"), with no lang="en" span wrapping it to flag the language switch to assistive tech.
findings.recommendation: Localize via useTranslations (a t("common.close") style key already exists in pattern with the rest of the codebase) or, if kept static, wrap it in `<span lang="en">`.
findings.industry_rationale: Minor on its own, but on a bilingual institutional site where Arabic-locale conformance is presumably part of the same accessibility bar as English, an unlocalized string breaks SC 3.1.2 (Language of Parts) and is a low-risk fix relative to the rest of this list.

findings.title: Back-to-top button remains keyboard-focusable while visually hidden (opacity-0, pointer-events-none)
findings.evidence: The button is always rendered; visibility is toggled purely via `visible ? "translate-y-0 opacity-100" : "pointer-events-none translate-y-3 opacity-0"` (line 33). There is no tabIndex={-1}, aria-hidden, or disabled applied when !visible, so before the user scrolls past 480px, the button sits in the natural tab order, fully invisible.
findings.recommendation: Either add `tabIndex={visible ? 0 : -1}` (and aria-hidden={!visible}) when hidden, or gate rendering on `visible` entirely (mount/unmount) rather than opacity-toggling a persistently-focusable element.
findings.industry_rationale: Lower severity than the Reveal bug because it's a single, non-critical utility control rather than primary content or lead-gen form fields, but it's the same underlying anti-pattern (focusable-but-invisible) appearing a second time independently in the codebase, suggesting a project-wide sweep is worthwhile.

findings.title: Not verified this session: mobile/small-viewport keyboard and touch-target accessibility
findings.area: All pages at <768px, particularly the MobileNav Sheet+Accordion pattern and form modals on small screens
findings.evidence: Per the task brief, the browser tool used this session could not reliably force a sub-desktop viewport, so mobile rendering of focus order, touch target sizing (WCAG 2.5.5/2.5.8), and the Sheet-based mobile nav's focus trap behavior were not observed live — only inferred from source (which looks reasonable: base-ui Sheet/Accordion primitives, aria-label on the trigger).
findings.recommendation: Run an actual mobile-viewport pass (real device or Chrome DevTools responsive mode with touch emulation) against the MobileNav sheet, the two lead-gen modals, and the Contact form before treating this lens as fully cleared — the DialogContent modals use `max-w-[calc(100%-2rem)]` with no explicit mobile-specific focus/scroll handling verified.
findings.industry_rationale: Flagging as an open item rather than a defect per the task's explicit instruction not to assert mobile is broken or fine without verification; institutional buyers reviewing on tablets in a hospital procurement office is a plausible real usage pattern worth confirming.

reports.summary: The lead-gen mechanics on EMC's detail-page templates (Solution, Product, Partner) are genuinely well built: every one ends in a consistent CtaBand, product pages layer Request a Demo / Speak with a Specialist / Download Brochure in the hero with correct visual hierarchy, and the forms collect real institutional-procurement fields (job title, department, procurement type: tender/direct) rather than generic consumer fields. The site also holds the line on the spec's hardest rule — it ships zero fabricated testimonials or stats, which matters for credibility with a technical buyer. But three things materially cap conversion today: (1) the three catalog/listing pages this audit was asked to focus on — Solutions, Products, Partners index — are the one place in the IA with no repeated lead-gen CTA at all, so a browsing visitor who doesn't click into a specific card hits a dead end; (2) the confirmed reveal.tsx scroll-animation bug is not a cosmetic curiosity for this audit — it sits directly on top of the home hero's headline, subhead, and both primary CTA buttons, and screenshot evidence shows it also washing out the real product photography on the Products listing page, i.e. it degrades the exact assets meant to carry the "Medtronic-tier" credibility bar and the exact buttons meant to convert; and (3) on code-verified mobile breakpoints (below 640px) the header's Request a Demo button is explicitly hidden with no equivalent CTA inside the hamburger menu, leaving WhatsApp as the only reliably-visible conversion path on a phone.
strengths: Every Solution/Product/Partner detail page template ends in a consistent CtaBand (Quotation Request + Contact EMC) — src/components/sections/cta-band.tsx, wired into all three [slug]/page.tsx files — so a visitor who reaches the bottom of any detail page always has a next step.

Product detail hero (src/app/[locale]/products/[slug]/page.tsx lines 106-121) shows three CTAs with genuinely correct visual hierarchy: Request a Demo (filled/primary), Speak with a Specialist (outline), Download Brochure (ghost, conditional) — textbook commitment-level sequencing, not a wall of equal-weight buttons.

Lead-gen forms (demo-request-modal.tsx, quotation-request-modal.tsx) collect fields that match how real institutional buyers actually work — organization, job title, department, city, procurementType: 'tender'|'direct' — rather than generic consumer form fields. Reads as built by someone who understands NUPCO/MOH procurement workflows.

Zero fabricated trust content: content/testimonials/ is empty and content/stats.json has all three counters marked verified:false, and both StatsBand and TestimonialsSection correctly render null rather than showing placeholder numbers or fake quotes. For a medical-adjacent B2B site this discipline is a real credibility asset, not just spec compliance.

22 real, named hospital/institution logos (NUPCO, Sulaiman Al Habib Medical Group, King Saud Medical City, Prince Sultan Military Medical City, etc.) are wired into a well-engineered marquee (customer-marquee.tsx) that pauses on hover/focus/drag, supports manual scroll, and falls back to a static wrapped grid under prefers-reduced-motion — genuinely relevant social proof for this exact buyer, not filler.

Site-wide floating WhatsApp FAB (whatsapp-fab.tsx) gives a low-friction, region-appropriate conversion channel that is plain HTML/CSS with no client-side animation dependency, so it is unaffected by the Reveal/hydration issues affecting other CTAs.

Partner relationship copy (e.g. partner detail page's relationshipStatement block) avoids fabricated exclusivity claims per the spec's hard rule — for a technically literate procurement audience that will fact-check distributorship claims, this restraint protects rather than costs credibility.

findings.title: Primary header CTA is hidden on mobile with no fallback in the hamburger menu
findings.evidence: src/components/layout/header.tsx line 55 wraps <DemoRequestModal /> in `<div className="hidden sm:block">` — below Tailwind's 640px breakpoint the Request a Demo button is not rendered at all, only the hamburger trigger is. src/components/layout/mobile-nav.tsx's sheet content (lines 43-98) contains only nav links (Home, Solutions accordion, Partners accordion, remaining primaryNav items) — no Request a Demo, Request a Quotation, or Speak with a Specialist action anywhere inside the mobile menu. This is a direct code reading, not an inference from the unverified mobile screenshots.
findings.recommendation: Add a persistent CTA (Request a Demo or Contact) either always-visible in the mobile header row (remove the sm:block gate, size it to fit next to the hamburger) or as a pinned action inside/below the mobile Sheet menu itself, so a phone visitor is never more than the hamburger tap away from converting.
findings.industry_rationale: This audience — biomedical engineers, ICU/anesthesia consultants, procurement managers — very plausibly first encounters EMC via a shared link or WhatsApp message on a phone, especially in Gulf B2B contexts where WhatsApp-first communication is the norm. Losing the primary CTA specifically on that channel, with no in-menu substitute, removes the intended conversion path for a segment of traffic the WhatsApp FAB alone won't fully substitute for (a specialist mid-procurement wants a structured Request a Quotation, not just a chat).

findings.title: The confirmed Reveal opacity bug sits directly on the home hero's headline, subhead, and both primary CTAs
findings.evidence: hero.tsx wraps the eyebrow+headline in one <Reveal>, the subhead in a second <Reveal delay={0.08}>, and the CTA row — Button 'Explore Our Solutions' + <DemoRequestModal> — in a third <Reveal delay={0.16}> (lines 25-45). Per the confirmed live bug in reveal.tsx, this whileInView-based wrapper frequently stays at opacity:0 on fresh load until the user scrolls. That means the single highest-value real estate on the site — headline, subhead, and both conversion buttons on first paint — is the content most exposed to this bug, not a peripheral element.
findings.recommendation: Treat this as the top-priority fix flowing from the already-confirmed reveal.tsx bug: at minimum, stop wrapping above-the-fold hero content (headline/subhead/CTAs) in scroll-triggered Reveal at all — content already in the viewport on load should render visible immediately, with Reveal reserved for content that starts below the fold. This also directly reduces the bug's blast radius even before the root IntersectionObserver/hydration timing issue is fixed.
findings.industry_rationale: A hospital administrator or procurement contact evaluating an unfamiliar vendor site decides in seconds whether to keep reading. If the first thing they see is a blank or half-rendered hero with invisible CTA buttons, the most likely outcome for a skeptical institutional buyer is not 'wait and scroll' — it's leaving, which is unrecoverable lost lead volume with no funnel-stage data to diagnose it.

findings.title: Solutions, Products, and Partners index (listing) pages end with no lead-gen CTA at all
findings.area: Solutions index, Products index, Partners index (src/app/[locale]/{solutions,products,partners}/page.tsx)
findings.evidence: All three index page.tsx files were read in full: solutions/page.tsx ends after the SolutionCard grid (line 71-74, closing tag immediately after RevealGroup); products/page.tsx ends after <ProductCatalog .../> (line 63-66); partners/page.tsx adds a 'Partner With Us' pillar section but that section (lines 70-95) is pure text/icon cards with no button, link, or modal anywhere in it. Compare this to every [slug] detail page, which imports and renders <CtaBand> at the bottom without exception.
findings.recommendation: Add the same CtaBand (or a lighter variant) to the bottom of all three index pages, and additionally surface a 'Can't find what you need? Speak with a specialist' prompt in the Products catalog's empty/no-results state (product-catalog.tsx line 147-150 currently just shows plain text 'No results').
findings.industry_rationale: These are precisely the pages named in this audit's brief, and they are also the most likely entry point for a procurement visitor doing comparison research across a catalog before deciding whom to contact — the classic 'browsing, not yet committed to one item' visitor a CTA at the bottom is designed to catch. Ending in silence after a card grid, with only the header CTA as a path forward, drops that visitor without a next step at the exact page type engineered to build purchase intent.

findings.title: Request a Quotation — the CTA type most relevant to procurement/tender buyers — only appears at the very bottom of product detail pages
findings.evidence: The hero CTA row (lines 106-121) offers only Request a Demo, Speak with a Specialist, and Download Brochure. QuotationRequestModal does not appear until the CtaBand at the very bottom (line 343), after gallery, videos, overview, clinical applications, key benefits, features, a technical specs table, certificates, downloads, related products, and a manufacturer card — a long scroll on a spec-heavy page.
findings.recommendation: Add a visible (even if secondary/outline) Request a Quotation action to the product hero CTA row alongside Demo/Specialist/Brochure, so tender-driven and direct-purchase procurement visitors — arguably the dominant intent type named in the audience brief (NUPCO, MOH, hospital procurement managers) — aren't required to scroll the entire spec sheet to find the CTA that matches their actual task.
findings.industry_rationale: The content model itself (Section 8.8 in PROJECT_SPEC.md) distinguishes procurementType: 'tender'|'direct' as a first-class field, showing the business already knows quotation requests are a distinct, high-value intent from demo requests. The page layout doesn't yet reflect that same prioritization at the point of highest attention (the hero).

findings.title: Reveal bug visibly degrades the site's one instance of real editorial device photography
findings.evidence: Screenshot 5 (Products listing, fully rendered per capture) shows all three visible product photographs rendered at what looks like roughly 15-20% opacity — a washed-out, ghostly appearance — while every other UI element (heading, filters, search bar) is fully opaque. product-catalog.tsx wraps each ProductCard in <Reveal delay={i * 0.05}> (line 139), which matches the known reveal.tsx symptom exactly: content frozen mid-fade until a scroll gesture fires the viewport check.
findings.recommendation: Same root-cause fix as the hero finding — but call out specifically that the Products grid is the page where the project's real, on-brand medical photography lives; regressing exactly that content undercuts the one section of the site currently hitting the stated 'Medtronic/Stryker-tier' visual bar.
findings.industry_rationale: The project brief explicitly measures the visual bar against large editorial photography of real devices. A washed-out first impression of that photography — on the page a comparison-shopping procurement visitor is most likely to linger on — works directly against the stated positioning shift away from looking like 'a regional distributor.'

findings.title: Home page's two dedicated trust-signal sections (Stats, Testimonials) currently render nothing
findings.evidence: content/stats.json has all three entries (years-of-experience, products, partners) marked verified:false with value:null, and StatsBand returns null when the filtered list is empty (stats-band.tsx line 15). content/testimonials/ contains zero JSON files, and TestimonialsSection returns null when empty (testimonials-section.tsx line 16). Both are correctly wired per the anti-fabrication rule — this is a content gap, not a code defect — but the net effect is that two of the nine sections laid out in home/page.tsx currently contribute zero content to the live page.
findings.recommendation: This is a business/content action item, not an engineering one: prioritize getting EMC to supply at minimum one or two real, attributable customer quotes and confirmed figures for years-of-experience/products/partners counts, since the code path to display them the moment they exist is already built and compliant.
findings.industry_rationale: For a credentialed technical buyer weighing an unfamiliar vendor, quantified scale (years operating, number of hospitals served, number of products) and named-source testimonials are exactly the kind of substantiating detail that converts skepticism into a demo request — more so than for a consumer audience. Right now the homepage has real logos (strong) but no accompanying numbers or voices to reinforce them.

findings.title: Generic gradient-blob hero visuals on About and Solution-detail pages, in place of photography
findings.area: About page hero, Solution detail hero (e.g. Anesthesia & Airway Management)
findings.evidence: Screenshot 4 (About hero) and screenshot 8 (Anesthesia & Airway Management solution hero) both show an abstract purple/teal gradient mesh (GradientMesh component, confirmed imported in solutions/[slug]/page.tsx line 18 and used at line 115) filling the entire visual half of the hero, with no photography or product imagery at all.
findings.recommendation: Prioritize sourcing or licensing editorial photography for the About hero and for solution categories that already have substantiated content (Anesthesia & Airway Management, per PROJECT_SPEC 9.3) — reserve GradientMesh strictly for the 'expanding' solution categories (Critical Care, Respiratory Care) where no real imagery exists yet, so the placeholder pattern reads as an honest 'coming soon' signal rather than the site's default visual language on pages that do have real content.
findings.industry_rationale: About and the two substantiated solution pages are high-consideration pages for this audience — a hospital administrator vetting a technology partner, or a clinician evaluating a specific clinical category, is exactly the visitor for whom the stated 'Medtronic/Stryker/Dräger' visual bar matters most. A generic gradient in that exact spot reads as unfinished/placeholder rather than as a deliberate accent, which works against the credibility-building goal of these particular pages.

findings.title: Header CTA, search, and language switcher appear absent on the very first hero screenshot capture
findings.evidence: Screenshot 1 (home hero, described as a fresh full render) shows the nav row ending at 'Contact' with no search icon, language switcher, or Request a Demo button visible in the remaining space of header width, whereas screenshots 2, 4, 5, and 7 (all captured after scroll or client-side navigation) show all three consistently. header.tsx itself contains no Reveal/opacity-hiding logic for these elements (SearchTrigger, LanguageSwitcher, DemoRequestModal are plain client components), so this is most consistent with a hydration-timing race at first paint (e.g. Base UI's DialogTrigger render-prop pattern not yet mounted) rather than the same root cause as the confirmed Reveal bug — flagging as a distinct, lower-confidence observation for engineering to investigate rather than a fully diagnosed defect.
findings.recommendation: Investigate whether SearchTrigger/LanguageSwitcher/DemoRequestModal SSR to an empty/hidden state before client hydration completes (common with portal-based UI libraries). If so, render a static, non-interactive placeholder button server-side so the CTA is visually present (even if not yet clickable) at first paint.
findings.industry_rationale: Even a sub-second gap where the primary conversion button is invisible during the first paint compounds the Reveal-bug risk already documented for the hero content beneath it — the two issues together mean a meaningful window on load where neither the header nor hero conversion paths are visible.

findings.title: The homepage's one editorial content feature (UE Integrated Airway Management Platform) ends in 'Learn more', not a lead-gen CTA
findings.evidence: featured-technology.tsx lines 58-62: the section's only action is a Button linking to /partners/ue-medical labeled 'Learn more' — no Request a Demo or Request a Quotation option is offered directly from this section, despite it being explicitly called out in PROJECT_SPEC.md 9.1 as 'the only category with enough verified content to carry this treatment today.'
findings.recommendation: Add a secondary Request a Demo action next to the existing Learn More link, pre-filled with the UE Medical / Airway Management interest (the DemoRequestModal already supports a defaultInterest prop used elsewhere).
findings.industry_rationale: This is the single most substantiated, evidence-rich section on the homepage (real founding year, employee count, hospital count, R&D centers) — exactly the kind of specificity this audience responds to. Routing that peak-interest moment only to another content page, rather than offering the direct conversion action, is a missed capture point at the section built to be the homepage's strongest sell.

reports.lens: Healthcare B2B industry & brand-positioning fit — does the site read as a healthcare technology partner to a credentialed Gulf institutional buyer, or does it still read as a regional distributor?
reports.summary: The site's copy layer has genuinely made the positioning shift the spec asked for — the hero, About page, and Why EMC content consistently use partner/technology-transfer language (training, regulatory knowledge, after-sales service, SFDA/NUPCO literacy) instead of distributor language, and no stray "distributor" language exists anywhere in shipped content. The homepage hero also clears the visual bar with real, dignified clinical photography. But the shift breaks down as soon as a buyer clicks past the homepage: every interior page that would normally carry the "global technology partner" weight — About, all five Solution details, all Partner details, Product detail — falls back to an abstract purple/teal gradient blob (GradientMesh) instead of photography, which is the opposite of the "startup SaaS" look the brief's named benchmarks (Medtronic, Stryker, GE Healthcare, Philips, Karl Storz, Dräger) use. Combined with a confirmed scroll-reveal bug that leaves hero and section text at near-zero opacity until the user scrolls, a procurement contact or biomedical engineer evaluating EMC's credibility on the pages that matter most (Partner detail, Solution detail) is currently landing on a page that alternates between an invisible headline and a generic gradient block where evidence of real technology should be. The underlying content architecture (verified-only stats, empty-not-fabricated testimonials, attributed manufacturer claims) is disciplined and audience-appropriate; the execution gap is almost entirely in hero/visual treatment on interior pages, not in the writing.
strengths: Hero copy and About copy have fully executed the 'partner not distributor' repositioning: 'EMC connects Saudi and Gulf healthcare providers with the global medical technologies, clinical training, and technical support that make advanced care possible' (home hero, screenshot 1) and the About intro in content/pages/about.json line 9 name training, technical support, regulatory knowledge, and after-sales service explicitly — this is exactly the vocabulary the buyer persona (biomedical engineers, procurement) needs to differentiate EMC from a catalog reseller. A grep across content/components confirms 'distributor' does not appear anywhere in shipped copy.

The 'Why EMC' pillar content (content/pages/about.json, ~line 65) is written as evidence-oriented operating-model description rather than marketing slogan, per PROJECT_SPEC Section 9.6 — e.g. Training & Education ties directly to 'confident with it at installation,' and Regulatory Knowledge / the CEO bio explicitly cite SFDA requirements and NUPCO procurement, which is precisely the institutional vocabulary a MOH/NUPCO contact or hospital administrator is scanning for.

Product listing page copy (screenshot 5) states 'nothing is listed until EMC and the manufacturer confirm it' — a credibility-building line for a technical/regulatory-literate buyer, and it correctly avoids e-commerce framing entirely (no price, no cart; filter by solution/manufacturer/clinical application as spec'd).

Solutions are framed as clinical categories tied to named manufacturer partnerships ('Clinical categories built around real partnerships,' 'Five clinical categories, each built around a real manufacturer partnership rather than a catalog of unrelated products') — the correct IA move away from a flat product/logo grid and toward a partner-technology narrative, matching PROJECT_SPEC Section 7's resolved conflict.

The AMECO partner correction (recent commit) and the Partners cross-sell cards (screenshot 3) give real founding-year/ISO/facility-scale detail (1984, 30,000 sqm, ISO 13485:2016, CE) rather than vague 'trusted partner' filler — this is the specificity Section 3 of the spec asks for and reads credibly to a biomedical engineer.

The home hero uses real editorial OR photography (screenshot 1) with restrained purple/teal used only as an eyebrow label and button accent, not a background fill — on this one page the site actually hits the stated Medtronic/Stryker/GE visual bar.

The content architecture enforces the spec's anti-fabrication rules structurally, not just by convention (CustomersBand returns null when the customers array is empty, stats are verified-only, UE Medical claims are attributed as 'per UE Medical corporate materials') — for a medical-adjacent B2B buyer who will fact-check claims, this restraint is itself a trust signal even though it's invisible as a 'feature.'

findings.title: Every interior hero that should carry technology/credibility weight falls back to an abstract gradient blob instead of photography
findings.area: About, Solution detail (x5), Partner detail (x3), Product detail — src/components/sections/gradient-mesh.tsx, used in src/app/[locale]/about/page.tsx, src/app/[locale]/solutions/[slug]/page.tsx, src/app/[locale]/partners/[slug]/page.tsx, src/app/[locale]/products/[slug]/page.tsx, and src/components/sections/cta-band.tsx
findings.evidence: Screenshot 4 (About hero) and screenshot 8 (Anesthesia & Airway Management solution hero) both show a flat purple-to-teal rounded gradient rectangle in the position where the homepage (screenshot 1) shows real OR photography. A grep for 'GradientMesh' confirms it is imported in exactly the pages a credentialed buyer would use to evaluate EMC's substance: About, every Solution detail, every Partner detail, every Product detail, and the generic CTA band.
findings.recommendation: Treat this as the single highest-leverage fix for the positioning goal: source or commission real photography/device imagery for About and at least the two fully-substantiated solution pages (Anesthesia & Airway Management, backed by real UE Medical content) and the UE Medical partner page first, since those are the pages with enough verified content to carry an editorial photo treatment per PROJECT_SPEC Section 9.3. Reserve GradientMesh only for categories still in the honest 'expanding' placeholder state (Critical Care, Respiratory Care) so the visual abstraction itself signals 'content pending' rather than being used uniformly across a site claiming an editorial-photography bar.
findings.industry_rationale: The brief's own visual bar names benchmarks (Medtronic, Stryker, GE Healthcare, Philips, Karl Storz, Dräger) that never use flat gradient blocks for hero visuals — they use large, specific clinical or device photography because credentialed buyers (biomedical engineers, ICU consultants) are visually verifying 'is this a real technology company with real installed equipment' within seconds of landing. A generic gradient block reads as a placeholder or a pre-launch marketing site, reinforcing exactly the 'thin regional distributor' impression the rebuild is trying to shed — and it does so specifically on the Partner and Solution pages where that impression matters most.

findings.title: Confirmed scroll-reveal bug leaves hero/CTA text at near-invisible opacity on load, directly suppressing the lead-generation CTAs this site exists to drive
findings.area: src/components/motion/reveal.tsx (Reveal/RevealGroup), affecting Home, About, Products, Solutions listing, Solution detail, Contact
findings.evidence: Screenshot 8 (Anesthesia & Airway Management hero) shows the headline, subhead, and both CTA buttons ('Speak with a Product Specialist', 'Request a Demo') rendered at near-zero opacity — this is the reveal bug caught mid-state on a real page load, not a mockup.
findings.recommendation: The engineering fix itself is out of scope for this design-lens report (already root-caused to reveal.tsx's whileInView/IntersectionObserver timing), but it should be escalated as the top overall priority alongside the photography gap, because unlike a visual-taste issue it can make the primary conversion action (the CTA buttons that are the site's whole business model per Section 11) unreadable or unclickable-looking on first paint — a hospital administrator or procurement contact filling out the Contact form (screenshot 7) without scrolling first could similarly encounter invisible form labels.
findings.industry_rationale: This audience does not browse casually — a MOH/NUPCO or hospital-administrator visitor often arrives from a specific referral or tender requirement and is scanning for the fastest path to 'Request a Quotation' or 'Speak with a Specialist.' Any apparent brokenness at that exact moment reads as unprofessional for a company positioning itself as a serious technology partner to institutional buyers, and it directly suppresses the lead-generation metric the entire site is built around.

findings.title: Home mid-page reads as an icon-and-copy card grid, not the 'large editorial photography' treatment named in the brief
findings.evidence: The 'Clinical categories built around real partnerships' 5-card grid (screenshot 2) uses small line icons (Syringe, HeartPulse, Ambulance, Bandage, AirVent, per content/solutions/*.json 'icon' fields) inside pale teal rounded squares, with body copy below — no photography, no device imagery, no partner branding anywhere in the primary cross-sell surface between the hero and the rest of the page.
findings.recommendation: For the solution categories with real substantiated content (Anesthesia & Airway Management via UE Medical now; Orthopedics/Infection Control once Ortholand/BeneCare/OXY'PHARM copy exists), swap the icon tile for a small representative product or clinical-use photo in the card, keeping icons only for the categories still in the honest placeholder state (Critical Care, Respiratory Care) so the visual language itself signals 'this one is real, this one is expanding.'
findings.industry_rationale: Generic line-icon grids are the default pattern of nearly every SaaS/services marketing site; the named competitive set (GE Healthcare, Philips Healthcare, Karl Storz) differentiates clinical categories with device or procedure photography specifically because their buyers associate a named piece of hardware or a recognizable clinical scene with credibility faster than an abstract pictogram does.

findings.title: Why EMC is reduced to a single-paragraph teaser on the homepage, undercutting the differentiator the whole rebuild is centered on
findings.evidence: why-emc-teaser.tsx renders only an eyebrow, one headline, one body paragraph, and a single 'Learn more' link to /about#why-emc — none of the eight substantiated pillars (Clinical Expertise, Technical Support, Training & Education, After-Sales Service, Regulatory Knowledge, Fast Response, Hospital Partnership, Quality Assurance) that already exist as real copy in content/pages/about.json are surfaced on the homepage itself.
findings.recommendation: Promote 3-4 of the strongest pillars (Training & Education, Regulatory Knowledge, Technical Support, After-Sales Service) into a compact icon-row or 2x2 grid directly in this homepage section, since that content already exists and is spec-compliant (evidence-oriented, not slogan-y). Right now a buyer has to click through to /about to encounter the actual substance of 'why partner not distributor,' which is the single most important idea the rebuild needs to land on the page most visitors will actually read.
findings.industry_rationale: A procurement or administrator-level visitor evaluating multiple vendors typically will not click past the homepage on a first pass; the 'partner vs. distributor' differentiation needs to be legible from the homepage scroll, not gated behind a second click, especially since the underlying content proving the differentiation (SFDA/NUPCO literacy, hands-on training model) is already written and simply isn't surfaced here.

findings.title: Homepage partners band is a plain logo row with generic framing, while the actual credibility markers (founding year, ISO, facility scale) only appear one click deeper
